title: Ravens Week 6 hangover discussion: level of concern after loss to Browns
summary: The Baltimore Ravens lost their second game of the season on Sunday afternoon, again to an opponent they should have beat. They has gone 1-1 in Lamar Jackson’s absence due to an ankle injury that will continue to loom over the team until he is back on the field. Losing to the Cleveland Browns – […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Head coach Jesse Minter of the Baltimore Ravens looks on against the Cleveland Browns during the third quarter of the game at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens lost their second game of the season on Sunday afternoon, again to an opponent they should have beat. They has gone 1-1 in Lamar Jackson’s absence due to an ankle injury that will continue to loom over the team until he is back on the field. Losing to the Cleveland Browns – and letting them secure first place in the AFC North for the first time since 2014 – is nothing to be proud of. But is the sky really falling in Baltimore, or are these standard struggles for a team missing several key players, including a two-time MVP quarterback? How concerned are you coming out of Sunday’s defeat? Nikhil’s take: Let’s be honest: the excitement of the Ravens’ fourth-quarter comeback and overtime win in Atlanta overshadowed three other quarters of uninspiring play from Tyler Huntley. He carried his hot streak into the first quarter of Sunday afternoon’s game (with some major assists from Declan Doyle and Josh Cuevas), but his ‘gamer’ magic was nowhere to be found for the last three. Nothing limits an offense like a weakened unit up front and a backup quarterback who struggles to push the ball downfield, and Baltimore dealt with both in Cleveland. In the past, the Ravens needed Lamar Jackson back on the field so he could don his superhero cap and carry the offense. This time, he just needs to run it with a full playbook that threatens defenses at all levels of the field. Doyle could not find the answers for the Browns’ aggression on Sunday, largely because he was missing a pantry staple. It’s not a secret sauce – Baltimore’s offense does not need Jackson to turn every play into backyard football – they just need their standard ingredients. Defensively, the Ravens buried the Browns in the first half before spending two-thirds of the second half of the field – and playing like it down the stretch. This is an under-discussed element of Baltimore’s collapses: the offense cannot sustain drives, leading to disparities in play count and time of possession that tank the defense late. But looking at the entire game, they played well enough to win. The Ravens have a tough stretch coming up that will test their mettle. That and staying healthy are my two primary concerns moving forward. But Sunday afternoon’s loss did not change either of those factors, and there is plenty of reason to believe this team can get better. They have not been at full strength this year, and next week could be their first game with Jackson, Ja’Kobi Lane, Trey Hendrickson, and Nnamdi Madubuike all playing. Let’s see how that looks before drawing any sweeping conclusions.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Top takeaways from the Ravens’ loss to the Browns in Week 6
summary: The Baltimore Ravens dropped their first divisional game of the season, losing a sloppy 13-10 affair in Cleveland after the Browns hit a walk-off field goal. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s top takeaways from the sluggish defeat: The Ravens need a real quarterback … Look, we all love Snoop, but after his gutsy performance in Atlanta, […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens runs with the ball against the Cleveland Browns during the first quarter of the game at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens dropped their first divisional game of the season, losing a sloppy 13-10 affair in Cleveland after the Browns hit a walk-off field goal. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s top takeaways from the sluggish defeat: The Ravens need a real quarterback … Look, we all love Snoop, but after his gutsy performance in Atlanta, the Ravens got the worst version of him in Cleveland. Tyler Huntley wasn’t helped by a slow offensive operation and plenty of pressure from the Browns’ defensive front, but he put the ball in danger too often and could not move the chains on third down. This offense is just so limited with him under center that the rest of the offense has to execute flawlessly, and that’s just not going to happen when the defense can constantly overload the box against the run. Huntley’s usual magic was nowhere to be found on Sunday, but Lamar Jackson wins that game handily. The Ravens need him back for their tough string of upcoming opponents. — Nikhil Mehta … And the Ravens need a real center Again, utmost respect to Vega Ioane for sliding to center for three starts, but the Ravens have clearly been playing with fire. The first-round pick’s inconsistent snapping nearly led to a fumble during a crucial second-half drive. Huntley managed to dive on the football, but the play turned a 2nd-and-19 into a 3rd-and-22 that all-but-guaranteed a punt on 4th down. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle definitely needs to clean up his playcalling operation, but having a backup QB and a rookie guard-turned-center is not ideal for pre-snap communication. Enter trade acquisition Cam Jurgens, who should be ready for his Ravens debut next week. He’ll help the entire unit at the line of scrimmage, snap the ball cleanly, and, crucially, move Ioane back to right guard to get Emery Jones off the field. — Nikhil Mehta Kyle Hamilton and Nnamdi Madubuike deserve bette r I could probably throw other names in here, but Hamilton and Madubuike were the best players on the field on Sunday afternoon. They carried their entire team for stretches of the game with disruptive play around the line of scrimmage against the run and the pass. I almost feel bad watching them field questions about another second-half defensive collapse. They’re good teammates who won’t throw the offense under the bus, even though most of the blame belongs on that side of the ball. Hamilton, who has taken Roquan Smith’s mantle as the defense’s de facto leader, looks especially pained when he has to answer for a loss despite another All-Pro performance. Madubuike, meanwhile, has impressively come all the way back from last year’s neck injury to recapture his previous elite form. But they can’t make every play for the defense, nor can they will the offense to score. — Nikhil Mehta It’s time for Mark Andrews to lose snaps Anyone watching lately can tell Mark Andrews has been caught at the scene of the crime too often, but that alone isn’t why I think this. Even the simple plays are proving costly: Andrews has six drops through six games. Fortunately, rookie TEs Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas have shown flashes of playmaking that Andrews no longer has at 31. In addition to the flashes, the young TE duo have had steady hands, hauling in 12 of their combined 13 targets, with two touchdowns to Andrews’ one. Cuevas flashed in today’s loss, catching his first NFL touchdown along with a 29-yard catch-and-run from an impressive Declan Doyle play call that saw Cuevas line up at left guard pre-snap. Hibner made noteworthy plays against Dallas and Tennessee. I expect Andrews to continue to lead the unit in snaps if Hibner stays sidelined. However, as soon as both rookie tight ends are available, they should be cutting into the veteran tight end’s snap count. — Mark Myers The Ravens need more efficiency in the run game Entering today’s game, the Ravens ranked No. 3 in rushing yards per game, averaging 164.4 yards on the ground with 822 total. However, their efficiency has left much to be desired in recent weeks and Derrick Henry in particular has found running room hard to come by often. Against the Browns, Henry rushed for a season-low 58 yards on 17 carries (3.4 yards per carry). Since Week 1, Henry has not eclipsed 4.3 yards per carry in a game and over the last three weeks, his longest rush has gone for just 17 yards. Too often it feels like Henry is running into a wall of defenders for minimal gain, which has happened at times in high-stakes short yardage attempts on third or fourth down. The Ravens have not been able to open up gaping holes for Henry to rip off breakaway runs as has usually been the case over the past couple years. Justice Hill had a 47-yard rush in Week 5 lined up in the fullback spot, but that has been the Ravens’ only big explosive run in a while. They need to be more consistent at the line of scrimmage in their run blocking, and Henry also needs to ensure he won’t lose any more fumbles in key moments like he did in the fourth quarter of this game — Frank Platko
author: Mark Myers

title: Ravens postgame discussion: instant reactions to Week 6 loss to the Browns
summary: The Baltimore Ravens let yet another double-digit second-half lead slip away in Sunday’s 13-10 loss to the Cleveland Browns with Andre Szmyt kicking a game-winning field goal as time expired. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s instant reactions: Nikhil Mehta Last week, the Ravens got the best of the Tyler Huntley experience. He had his usual limitations, […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Andre Szmyt #25 of the Cleveland Browns kicks the game winning field goal to defeat the Baltimore Ravens in the game at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens let yet another double-digit second-half lead slip away in Sunday’s 13-10 loss to the Cleveland Browns with Andre Szmyt kicking a game-winning field goal as time expired. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s instant reactions: Nikhil Mehta Last week, the Ravens got the best of the Tyler Huntley experience. He had his usual limitations, but he flipped the ‘gamer’ switch in the fourth quarter to secure the comeback win. But in Cleveland, Snoop just could not get the job done. He was lucky to finish this game without multiple interceptions on an underwhelming stat sheet that features just 165 yards on 31 passing attempts. Despite an encouraging start, the offensive operation was a mess all afternoon, heightening the importance of getting Lamar Jackson and Cam Jurgens on the field. Baltimore’s defense will be hard on themselves for giving up another double-digit second-half lead, but the offense consistently put them in tough positions. Kyle Hamilton and Nnamdi Madubuike nearly carried the Ravens to a win on their own today, but none of their teammates could dig deep and come up with a play when they needed it most. However, I’m not coming out of this game with any sweeping conclusions. The alarm bells aren’t going off. The coaching and talent is there; the Ravens just need to get (and stay) healthy to let it shine. Zach Canter Weird things happen in Cleveland, every year, every time. It’s hard to overcome them like the Ravens tend to do when you don’t have Lamar Jackson. Derrick Henry fumble, a Tyler Loop miss, an awful DPI that was picked up, a penalty on Cleveland that was picked up after being announced. Defense did its job for the most part. All the score came from close range but the third down defense was still highly disappointing in the fourth quarter. The offense is the real issue. They had two fantastic drives and then decided to clock out for the day. The offensive line was moved for most of the day, pass catchers dropped the ball a ton, Derrick Henry didn’t do much, and Tyler Huntley was highly inaccurate multiple times. Simply not good enough. Stephen Bopst Very ugly game all around. The Ravens were in control early but made enough mistakes to give the Browns the game. Derrick Henry’s fumble and Tyler Loops missed field goal proved to be their undoing along with some typical questionable calls from the refs down the stretch. Somehow replay assist was used to overturn a Browns penalty but was not for a terrible DPI on Keyon Martin. After the first two drives, the offense was truly terrible and badly need their starting QB back. With even a below average performance from them, the Ravens probably win this. The Ravens have now lost possession of first place in the division and head into the most pivotal part of their schedule. Kevin McNelis No one to blame but themselves. We say this over and over and over again, and here we are. In the first quarter, the Ravens took a 10-0 lead and had a lot of good things going for them. The defense was providing shutdown coverage through the air, and while it was a slog to get things going, it had the potential to be a low-scoring win if they could just gut it out. In order to gut out a win, though, you need the guts to do it. This version of this team sorely lacked guts today. As soon as the Loop kick sailed wide, I knew they were in trouble. We’ve seen the trends in games with the missed kicks, inability to adjust away from a struggling run game leading to a Henry fumble, Charmin Ultra-Soft coverage in the secondary, all aided by atrocious officiating favoring the home team, and the Ravens drop a game that they had every opportunity to win. Anthony Weaver and that secondary have a lot of soul searching to do after this one. The O-line desperately needs help and if LJ isn’t ready to go, the coaching staff should have a serious conversation about Joe Fagnano starting in favor of Snoop next week. My parting shot: RUN PLAY ACTION. If eight defenders are stacked in the box to slow down your future HOF running back, someone is open downfield. It’s not rocket science and I feel like we never see it unless LJ is in. Mark Myers A brutal ending that unfortunately everyone could see coming from the moment Tyler Loop missed wide left. The Ravens of old showed up today, putting up zero points in the final three quarters while mixing in crucial errors. As tough as it is, the solutions are simple. Lamar Jackson will need to return next week to get the team back on track as they begin a stretch of tough opponents. Dustin Cox This was a typical, ugly divisional game on the road and the Ravens ended up on the wrong side of it at the end. For as much praise as Tyler Huntley rightly received after his late-game heroics against the Falcons, he deserves just as much criticism this week for a truly dreadful performance. Baltimore’s offense was completely stagnant after a strong first quarter saw them go up 10-0. The defense did their job to the best of their ability considering the positions they were put into by the offense. Derrick Henry’s fumble and Tyler Loop’s missed field goal were the biggest blunders of the day for the Ravens, but there were plenty of smaller errors that culminated in a game this team needs to quickly forget. The hope now is that Lamar Jackson can return to practice, because it is hard to envision this team beating the Bengals with another offensive performance similar to this one. Now, it’s your turn! Give us your instant reaction to the Ravens’ loss in the comments section below!

title: 3 Keys to Victory for Ravens-Browns Week 6
summary: The Ravens look to keep their win streak going in their first divisional tilt of the season, heading up to Cleveland. The Browns look like a heavily improved squad with a ton of young, rookie-contract players helping lead the way to Cleveland’s 3-2 record. The Ravens will be without Lamar Jackson in this one so […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 11: Baltimore quarterback Tyler Huntley (5) rolls out to pass during the NFL game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Atlanta Falcons on October 11th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Ravens look to keep their win streak going in their first divisional tilt of the season, heading up to Cleveland. The Browns look like a heavily improved squad with a ton of young, rookie-contract players helping lead the way to Cleveland’s 3-2 record. The Ravens will be without Lamar Jackson in this one so it’ll be Tyler Huntley once more leading the charge, hoping to keep his undefeated streak in starts since last year going. A faster start on offense Tyler Huntley and the Ravens offense were fantastic at the end of the game against the Atlanta Falcons. The last drive to tie it in regulation and the overtime drive were simply masterful. But there was also a feeling that the Ravens left a lot on the table last week. Despite Atlanta leading the game most of the time, it felt like Baltimore was in control most of the time, especially on defense, and they just couldn’t punch in the scores to match that. There were some other reasons for that – Mark Andrew’s drops and fumbles chief among them – but the offense also had plenty of three-and-outs and short drives that killed any moment the defense built with stops. Huntley struggled early to be decisive when it came to pulling the trigger or deciding to just take off and run. In a division game that always gets weird in Cleveland every year, the Ravens offense needs to put points up faster. They settled for field goals far too often early and took till midway through the third quarter before finally punching it in the endzone. This isn’t to say go for it on fourth down and skip the field goals. Take the points when you can. But the Ravens need to find the endzone faster. I expect a similar game plan to last week. A lot of short stuff predicated on Zay Flowers’ movement and attention on Derrick Henry, with heavy involvement from Rashod Bateman and Mark Andrews. But let’s get some deep shots in this week when the secondary inevitably creeps up. Ja’Kobi Lane is finally returning. Throw him a couple jump balls and give Tez Walker a shot or two deep. Focus on KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston The two rookie wide receivers have been simply sensational. Second-round pick Boston has led the way so far, being an incredible deep threat with multiple long touchdowns. He’s capable of getting vertical quickly, has strong hands and contested catch ability, and can break multiple tackles to extend the play. Concepcion has continued to be the do-it-all weapon he was at Texas A&M that made him a first-round pick. He can run every route in the tree at every level, is capable of doing all the gadgety stuff in an offense with motion, and is a weapon after the catch with punt returner skills. He’s a very similar player to Zay Flowers, the biggest difference being Flowers has better movement ability and Concepcion has more ideal size. These wideouts have changed Cleveland’s offense dramatically and have taken over the wide receiver room already as rookies. They, along with tight end Harold Fannin, are helping lead Cleveland’s recent renaissance in the passing offense. Last week, the Ravens plan was clearly to load the box, stop Bijan Robinson, and make Michael Penix beat them through the air to Drake London. This week, the Ravens should return to their normal style of play: light boxes, no over-the-top throws, and forcing teams to go the long way with consistent short passes and correct quarterback decision-making. Take advantage of the Browns’ injuries Just like the Ravens are bruised and battered, the Browns might be just as much, if not more so. The Browns will be missing Mason Graham in this one, who’s taken over as the lead dog in the front seven after Myles Garrett’s trade to LA. Graham currently leads the Browns in sacks and is a pure three-down defensive lineman force. It’s a massive loss for the Browns in this one and should contribute to helping keeping Huntley clean and allowing the Ravens to run the ball, something they haven’t been able to do in a couple of seasons. The Browns are also missing their lead running back, Quinshon Judkins, while linebacker Carson Schwesinger is playing hurt. Both were part of last year’s excellent rookie class for the Browns, and both only practiced limited once during the week. It should make the Ravens’ job easier to focus on the Browns’ receivers, with the Browns’ run game significantly hampered. The Ravens will also have an easier time running the ball and using Huntley as a weapon without Schwesinger on the field as often or at all.
author: Zach Canter

title: Ravens discussion: predictions for Week 6 vs. Browns
summary: The Baltimore Ravens (4-1) have their first AFC North clash on Sunday afternoon, taking on the Cleveland Browns (3-2) in a potential revenge game for Todd Monken. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s predictions for the divisional matchup: Nikhil Mehta I thought the Falcons were the wrong matchup at the wrong time for the Ravens in Week […]
full_text: The Baltimore Ravens (4-1) have their first AFC North clash on Sunday afternoon, taking on the Cleveland Browns (3-2) in a potential revenge game for Todd Monken. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s predictions for the divisional matchup: Nikhil Mehta I thought the Falcons were the wrong matchup at the wrong time for the Ravens in Week 5, but Baltimore won the battle in the trenches on both sides of the ball and ground out a win. The Browns, especially with their injuries, feel like the kind of team that the Ravens should be able to handle, even without Lamar Jackson. Their ability to pull away will be predicated on cleaning up their mistakes on the margins – drops, penalties, and the like – and I would love to see Jesse Minter make a statement win in his first divisional game, against Todd Monken, no less! X-factor: Mark Andrews. Despite last week’s struggles, Tyler Huntley is still going to look for his veteran tight end throughout the game. Andrews is also the Ravens’ best inline blocker, which is especially crucial this week with Matt Hibner sidelined by a hand injury. If he can do the dirty work in the run game and move the chains through the air, Baltimore should be able to move the ball consistently. Score prediction: Ravens 23, Browns 13 Kevin McNelis The Ravens face a division opponent for the first time this season, and will do so on the road and without Lamar Jackson under center. Earlier in the week, there was some optimism that Baltimore could get LJ back, but as the week progressed with no appearances from Lamar at practice, the oddsmakers began to frame this game as more of a coin flip. The Ravens enter the game as 3-point road favorites. Cleveland wants this one badly as they sit just one game behind Baltimore in the division. They’re going to hit the Ravens with everything they’ve got, and Todd Monken’s familiarity with Baltimore’s personnel could lend itself to some offensive success, but Cleveland needs help on that side of the ball, and I don’t know that familiarity with their opponent is going to be enough. The Browns are 29th in total yards, and despite the emergence of young receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston, they’ve struggled mightily at times to push the ball downfield. You’ll see Baltimore’s secondary get hit for deep shots a time or two, but I feel like this game sees the Ravens reel in multiple picks. Looking at Cleveland’s games so far, I think their highest-caliber opponent was Jacksonville in Week 1, a game in which the Browns got smoked. The Jags made that game look easy, and I’d argue the Ravens have a better all-around roster than Jacksonville does, with the caveat that Baltimore is still relying on the services of a back-up QB. The Ravens have enough talent to win this game, and hopefully they can take advantage of both forced and unforced errors to get an important AFC North win on the road. X-factor: Justice Hill. The Browns have a decent defensive unit, so pass protection is going to be key. Justice Hill plays a huge part in pass pro, and while he made some big plays against Atlanta last week, some of my favorite highlights were ones where he knocked a guy’s chinstrap loose on a block. Look for him to help buy time for Snoop to operate. Score prediction: Ravens 21, Browns 17 Dustin Cox I predict the first truly elite game of the season for the Ravens’ defense against the Browns. Cleveland has struggled to run the ball this season, and with Quinshon Judkins questionable to play, I do not expect that to change against Baltimore. This means Deshaun Watson will likely have to take the game into his own hands by winning in the passing game. The Ravens will have to worry about a pair of talented rookie wide receivers in Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion, with Boston in particular presenting a dangerous downfield threat to Baltimore’s secondary. The Ravens’ defense has explosive plays through the air so far this season, while Boston has quickly made a name for himself on big plays down the field. I predict a strong showing from Baltimore’s pass rush with Trey Hendrickson back in the lineup alongside an ascending Mike Green on the opposite edge and Nnamdi Madubuike wreaking havoc on the interior. Offensively, I expect another heavy dose of Derrick Henry on the ground. Tyler Huntley will need to carry the momentum from his final drives against the Falcons into this week. I predict a touchdown for Ja’Kobi Lane in his first game back since Week 1. X-factor: Marlon Humphrey. He could find himself matched up with Boston throughout the game, which present a potentially favorable matchup for Watson to target deep down the field. Score prediction: Ravens 20, Browns 10 Frank Platko With a backup quarterback in a raucous divisional game, it’s unfair to expect the Ravens to replicate last week’s 30-point offensive performance. Thus, they will need a defensive-led victory. This is a favorable matchup for the Ravens on paper, but weird things can happen in AFC North battles. The key for Jesse Minter’s defense will be to keep Deshaun Watson in structure. He’s made plays this year when scrambling and evading pressure. Otherwise, the Browns’ offense has been very pedestrian. X-factor: Zay Flowers. Flowers is a major x-factor for the Ravens every week. However, he will be especially important in this game. The Browns play aggressive man coverage and will likely take away underneath passing routes. Flowers will need to continue getting open quickly to provide an outlet for Huntley, and create yards after the catch. Score prediction: Ravens 20, Browns 16 Now, it’s your turn! Add your prediction and X-factor for the Ravens-Browns game in the comments below!

title: 5 Questions about Ravens-Browns with Dawgs By Nature
summary: The Baltimore Ravens are taking on the Cleveland Browns on Sunday afternoon with their sights set on their fifth win of the season and second in a row with Tyler Huntley under center. To get the lowdown on Todd Monken’s squad, Baltimore Beatdown spoke with Dawgs By Nature’s Chris Pokorny and asked him five questions […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken looks on during the first half against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Robert Deutsch-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens are taking on the Cleveland Browns on Sunday afternoon with their sights set on their fifth win of the season and second in a row with Tyler Huntley under center. To get the lowdown on Todd Monken’s squad, Baltimore Beatdown spoke with Dawgs By Nature’s Chris Pokorny and asked him five questions about the Browns. Here are his answers: 1. When Todd Monken was hired as the Ravens’ OC, he was noted for his ability to scheme around his personnel. How has he done that in Cleveland? I think he’s brought that type of culture overall. I’ve told a few other sites this, but the top thing I hated about former head coach Kevin Stefanski and former defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz is that I never saw them make in-game adjustments, and would occasionally make them during a game. With Monken’s team, he encouraged competition to find the team’s best starting five offensive linemen, he’s not been afraid to lessen veteran Jerry Jeudy’s reps at the expense of the rookies, and I’m sure he has some oversight of the need to be willing to make adjustments to defensive gameplans during the game. 2. What parts of Monken’s scheme in Baltimore have carried over to the Browns offense? He doesn’t have the exact same personnel obviously, but he’s worked with another mobile quarterback and has more designed runs for him like you might have seen with Lamar Jackson. Monken has tried establishing a good rushing attack, but it hasn’t panned out well in the YPC department yet — but it still allows him to try dialing up those deep balls for explosive plays (namely to rookie WR Denzel Boston thus far). Overall, I think the offense still feels very different due to the personnel styles differing between the teams, but he’s making it work and hoping to achieve more success as time goes on. 3. The Ravens have been able to game plan around Myles Garrett in the past (though not always). Who is the Browns’ biggest pass-rushing threat now? The pressure has been coming from everyone, as ten different members of the Browns have registered at least one sack thus far (compared to just seven for the Ravens). Because it’s so spaced out, it’s hard to pick out the Browns’ biggest pass-rushing threat. You’d think that it would be Jared Verse, who came over from the Rams for Garrett, but he doesn’t even have a sack this year. Despite Verse’s numbers being down, he’s received a lot of praise from the defensive coaching staff for doing his job and helping free up the players around him. 4. Cleveland is dealing with a few injuries headed into Week 6. Which potential absences could have the biggest impact? My biggest question marks are surrounding DT Mason Graham and LB Carson Schwesinger, who are both questionable. They both returned in some capacity to practice on Friday, which is a positive sign. But the Browns also promoted two defensive tackles from the practice squad for Sunday’s game, and from a positional perspective, you usually think that’s a sign of depth issues at the position again (i.e. maybe they’ll give Graham’s knee injury another week to rest). Schwesinger seems more likely to play, but either of those players would be a huge detriment to the defense. Graham was playing at an All-Pro level for the first 3 weeks, and Schwesinger is coming off of his best game of the season. 5. Is there any chance that the Browns would consider a QB switch mid-game on Sunday? As crazy as it sounds — because fans hated the fact that Deshaun Watson was the starter heading into the season, and would’ve answered “absolutely yes” if this was asked back in Week 2 — but now, it would be a shock to see a quarterback switch mid-game for performance reasons. Watson helped get the Browns to 3-1, and even though last week was a rough performance for everyone in rainy conditions, he technically led a go-ahead touchdown drive again mid-way through the fourth quarter. Watson has done a solid job of using his legs to pick up key yards, and when he’s at his best, he’s taking the easy/smart yards underneath on passes, and then occasionally going for the longer ball. He almost seems like a game manager at times, but it’s definite growth from what he was doing for the Browns prior to his Achilles’ injuries.

full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 04: Philadelphia Eagles offensive lineman Cam Jurgens (51) warms up before the game between the Washington Commanders and Philadelphia Eagles on January 04, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Kyle Ross/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Baltimore Ravens fans largely approved of the team’s blockbuster trade for center Cam Jurgens with 75% of respondents to this week’s SB Nation Reacts grading the move at a B or higher. Of the other 25%, only 3% graded the move as a D, and none gave it an F. Overall, the grade averaged out to a B-. Here are the full results: Fans favored general manager Eric DeCosta’s willingness to aggressively upgrade at the Ravens’ biggest position of need, but noted Jurgens’ injury history and the steep price of a second-round pick. Here are a few top responses: It’s a tough one to call, but a move had to be made and even bad teams don’t like trading away offensive linemen. So I’m glad EDC was willing to go after someone. Cost was heavy, risky trade. But our window is right now and they had to take a swing. – Jt7king The price seems high for Jurgen recent play (arguably out of position) but the Ravens are/were in a position of serious need. Center was an issue after Linderbaum left in free agency, but it’s a serious run of bad luck to lose the next three centers to injury. I’m going with a “C” because we don’t know how Jurgens will play and if he’ll stay healthy here. If he solidifies the position and plays out the year, a second rounder still feels expensive but worth it if it helps the Ravens make a playoff run. – hampstead38 Expert grades from around the NFL world varied wildly. ESPN’s Ben Solak and Matt Walder gave the Ravens a D+, criticizing DeCosta for a desperation overpay, while The Athletic’s Jeff Howe praised Jurgens’ potential short- and long-term impact. Personally, I see this as a pristine example of a fair NFL trade. The Eagles gave up a talented player on an affordable contract in return for a solid draft pick they need with an increasingly expensive roster. The Ravens paid the market price for a proven starting offensive lineman when they badly needed one. That is just good business between two of the league’s better GMs. Jurgens could not clear concussion protocol in time to play on Sunday, but he should be in line to make his Ravens debut next week, hopefully with Lamar Jackson back under center. Between the Jurgens acquisition and last week’s overtime victory over the Atlanta Falcons, fan confidence has rebounded since dropping to 28% after Jackson’s ankle injury in Week 5. The Ravens won that game, but losing Jackson on top of several other key players raised concerns about an early injury crisis in Baltimore. The team is not out of the woods yet – Jackson will not play in Week 6, nor will defensive tackle Broderick Washington and rookie tight end Matthew Hibner – but they will get outside linebacker Trey Hendrickson and rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane back on the field in Cleveland. The Ravens are three-point favorites over the Browns heading into Sunday’s game with a 39.5-point over/under projecting a low-scoring game ( via FanDuel Sportsbook ). A win would keep them in sole possession of first place in the AFC North heading into a tough three-game stretch against the Bengals, Bills, and Jaguars.

title: Josh Allen ties Jim Kelly’s Bills passing touchdown record
summary: Of all the ways Josh Allen could have tied Jim Kelly’s franchise record for career touchdown passes, a backhanded shovel pass to wide receiver Keon Coleman probably wasn’t on anyone’s list. However, that’s exactly how the Buffalo Bills quarterback made history Sunday afternoon in Las Vegas, NV.   Allen entered Sunday’s game with 256 combined […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NV - OCTOBER 18: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills reacts after a play against the Las Vegas Raiders during the second half of an NFL football game at Allegiant Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Of all the ways Josh Allen could have tied Jim Kelly’s franchise record for career touchdown passes, a backhanded shovel pass to wide receiver Keon Coleman probably wasn’t on anyone’s list. However, that’s exactly how the Buffalo Bills quarterback made history Sunday afternoon in Las Vegas, NV. Allen entered Sunday’s game with 256 combined passing touchdowns, just two behind Kelly’s 258. By the time Buffalo finished its 33-30 win over the Raiders, the two quarterbacks were tied on top of the franchise list. Touchdown No. 257 came in the second quarter, when Allen connected with wide receiver Khalil Shakir on a nine-yard pass. That brought his career total to 257, leaving him one away from Kelly. SHAKIR SIGHTING!!!! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/7vB2RSbSpn — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) October 18, 2026 Then, in the third quarter, Allen found himself facing 3rd & 8 from the Raiders’ 12-yard line with the Las Vegas defense closing in around him. He spun away from the pressure and, with defenders blocking running lanes, flipped an unbelievable backhanded shovel pass to Coleman in the end zone. The 12-yard touchdown gave Buffalo a 23-13 lead with 6:22 left in the third quarter. It also gave Allen career passing touchdown No. 258, tying Kelly’s franchise record. JOSH ALLEN DOING JOSH ALLEN THINGS!!!! 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/F0GGilwmd6 — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) October 18, 2026 While we can compare seasons – Kelly’s 11 to Allen’s nine – there’s the argument that a season is longer now than it was then. But when we look at games, Allen is still ahead of the Pro Football Hall of Fame Bills all-timer’s pace. Kelly played 160 regular-season and 17 postseason games over his 11 seasons in Buffalo. Allen has played 134 regular-season games and has 15 postseason appearances. That’s 28 less games. Kelly does still have the regular-season record, but it’s doubtful that will last the remainder of the 2026 NFL season. The quarterback who led the Bills to their only Super Bowl appearances has 237 touchdown passes in the regular season. Allen sits at 229.

title: Bills at Raiders Week 6 instant game analysis: Buffalo grinds out key win
summary: The Bills escaped Las Vegas with a 33-30 win and head into the bye week at 5-1. Here’s everything I wrote down along the way. 1st Half 2nd Half 1-0. Go Bills! Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - OCTOBER 18: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills looks to pass against the Las Vegas Raiders in the third quarter of a game at Allegiant Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Bills escaped Las Vegas with a 33-30 win and head into the bye week at 5-1. Here’s everything I wrote down along the way. 1st Half Ray Davis: kickoff return weapon. 40 yards this time. (Bills: 5 kickoff returns, 132 yards, long of 40) I like sitting DJ Moore here. He’ll be missed, but we can’t afford not having him for the real run. Good ball protection by James Cook. Two hands on it, as it should be. (22 carries, 95 yards, 1 TD, no fumbles) Also good to put Dalton Kincaid in the game early. He’s a difference maker, and Joe Brady must make defenses worry about him from the get-go. (8 targets, 7 catches, 38 yards) Wasting 2 timeouts in the first offensive drive is far from ideal. Bills’ PA rollout game continues to suffer. Keon Coleman and Dawson Knox ran routes in the same area. Josh Allen was surprised by Walker coming on a blitz on 3rd down. I expect better from him in those situations. Tyler Bass FG is good, 3-0 Bills. Tre Tucker with the first catch between the Bills’ LBs and Safeties for 15 yards and a 1st down. This defense needs the bye week badly, and I hope there are changes planned. More of the same from the defense in their 1st drive. Bend and then break. Goal-line run by Ashton Jeanty, Terrel Bernard had him for a stuff, but simply got outpowered. (Jeanty: 10 carries, 22 yards, 1 TD) Good next offensive drive by Buffalo. PA rollout again not giving Josh easy buttons, he buys time and ends up finding Joshua Palmer for a big gain, out of structure. Also out of structure, Ty Johnson is a weapon in the passing game. Two more catches by Kincaid on this drive, I love it. One was a screen. Used his big body to gain two extra yards after contact. Utilize your weapons. After putting O’Cyrus Torrence on his butt, Maxx Crosby pushes Josh right after he throws the ball. Bills’ QB asks for a penalty, Crosby trash-talks. I’ll certainly keep an eye on this matchup. Drive stalls in the red zone as Josh tried to force a backshoulder to Kincaid in the end zone. Great job by Stokes making a play on the ball there. Another good FG by Bass. 7-6 Raiders. Bills’ D gets off the field. Man coverage on 3rd down and great job by Davison Igbinosun. The rookie has committed some penalties, but also has had some impressive coverage snaps. I like it. Rather have him playing physical all the time than allowing catches in soft coverage. (3 pass breakups) Cook with a checkdown catch and the 1st down. Every time he catches the ball in space there’s a feeling he can bring it to the house. Brady gotta find ways to give him more opportunities in the passing game. (3 catches on 3 targets, 58 yards) Josh with a dart to Coleman for another 1st down. Keon appears for the first time in this game. Josh reads the Raiders’ defense like a book pre-snap, changes the play and goes swing pass to Cook in the flat. Another big gain. 25 offensive plays for the Bills in this game versus just 12 for the Raiders. Great screen pass to Khalil Shakir, Spencer Brown leads the way for the TD. 13-7 Bills. Offense looks unstoppable. (Shakir: 4 catches on 6 targets, 34 yards, 1 TD) No Terrel Bernard on the field for a couple of drives , and Bills’ coaches with boards on the sidelines to communicate before snaps. Communication has been a hot topic recently on this D. Raiders in the red zone and Bills’ D forces a 4th down. Raiders tried to go, but a false start kills their chance. FG is good, 13-10 Bills, 2 minutes left in the 1st half. Joshua Palmer with his weekly awful drop on a perfect pass by Allen on a 2nd down. It set up a sack on 3rd and 9 and gave the Raiders a new opportunity with 1:40 left. I wouldn’t mind never watching Palmer in a Bills uniform anymore, to be honest. C.J. Gardner-Johnson with a missed tackle on Brock Bowers, allowing the Raiders to get in FG range. CJGJ with an Unsportsmanlike Conduct penalty, what did he do there? Walked toward the Raiders’ players and spit on the guy? What’s wrong with this dude? Inadmissible. Ejected from the game. Hopefully nothing serious, he’s going to the locker room now. Another 1st down by the Raiders, Bowers with strong hands. Benford all over him, simply too big. title: Josh Allen, 5-1 Buffalo Bills continue finding ways to win close games
summary: It’s no secret that Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen is a superbly talented, generational player. With Allen, the Bills are always well-positioned to win every game at any moment. Yet, winning in the NFL is difficult. It’s true that the mark of a great team isn’t necessarily how dominant it performs in a blowout win, […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NV - OCTOBER 18: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Las Vegas Raiders during the second half of an NFL football game at Allegiant Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s no secret that Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen is a superbly talented, generational player. With Allen, the Bills are always well-positioned to win every game at any moment. Yet, winning in the NFL is difficult. It’s true that the mark of a great team isn’t necessarily how dominant it performs in a blowout win, but how well they play in a close victory. For Buffalo a third of the way through the 2026 NFL season, the title of “Finishers” suits them well. All but one game (a win vs. Detroit Lions Week 2 — 41-31) has come down to a single score’s difference. Wins against the Houston Texans in Week 1 (36-31), Los Angeles Chargers Week 3 (24-16), Los Angeles Rams Week 5 (37-34), and Las Vegas Raiders Week 6 (33-30) took all the mental fortitude, discipline, and dialed-in play they could muster in all three phases. Their only loss this season, also decided by a single score — 29-26 to the New England Patriots in Week 3 — further reveals that these Bills may play a heck of a lot more games in similar fashion. It’s possible that Buffalo’s remaining schedule finds them in high-scoring shootouts where even 30 points doesn’t feel as comfortable as one might expect. Allen is obviously a huge reason why the Bills win the games they do, especially when he’s good for at least one impossibly brilliant play at the goal line for six. However, he’s not the only one on that side of the ball who makes Buffalo a feared team. Running back James Cook III is a special player. He again played a key role in victory, finishing with 22 carries for 95 yards and a score, plus three catches for 58 yards. Better yet? Cook didn’t fumble, as I predicted he’d rebound with a strong performance . Then there’s wide receiver Keon Coleman, who’s really turned it on in year three. The Bills needed Coleman to step up when top wide receiver DJ Moore picked up a shoulder injury, and Coleman has impressed. He’s beginning to look like a receiver ready for a consistent spotlight, with hands fit for carrying diamonds across tight ropes and verticality for days. To address the pink elephant in the room: Yes, the defense is yet a work in progress, and will be so well into training camp next summer with defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard at the helm. That said, the defensive line and edge rushers are bigger disruptors now, and so many holdover players are more efficient in almost every scenario. As for the defensive backfield? The masterful play by top cornerback Christian Benford against tight end Brock Bowers can’t be over-discussed in the coming days. Bowers, of course, had a decent day — but only when going against anyone not named Benford, and most folks will sign up for four catches and 70 yards without a score going up against Bowers. CBS game analyst J.J. Watt pointed out Benford’s play several times, saying that he should be the only one covering Bowers. In key moments where Bowers was likely to have the biggest impact, Benford was his shadow playing expertly blanketed coverage. The hope is that Buffalo’s other defensive backs use Benford’s tape in Week 6 to raise their individual levels to the greater good. To be fair, the defense played much better in Las Vegas. There will always be those ready to bash even the slightest mistake out of Jim Leonhard’s group. That’s just life. There’s also lot of good to focus on out of the ashes of yet another close victory that might not have been so without more than a few key defensive stops. Were there moments where it appeared Buffalo couldn’t do a thing to stop Las Vegas’ passing attack? Certainly. Expecting a finished product at this point is foolish. The defense has made strides in pass coverage, and the difference in run defense is night and day compared to former head coach Sean McDermott’s system. Buffalo needed its defense to step up today, and it did just enough at the right moments to give Allen, Cook, and company a path to victory. For that alone, a toast should be raised toward a Bills stop unit so often under the microscope. Winning close games will better prepare this young team for a postseason run. They just have to keep winning to put that theory to a proper test.

title: Buffalo Bills stock up, stock down in win at Las Vegas Raiders
summary: It wasn’t always pretty, but the Buffalo Bills have escaped Sin City with a victory, defeating the Las Vegas Raiders 33-30 in a hard-fought contest. The Raiders put up a fight against our Bills, but ultimately, it was one turnover that made the difference, and fortunately for the Bills, it was forced by the guys […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - OCTOBER 12: C.J. Gardner-Johnson #22 of the Buffalo Bills lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on October 12, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images It wasn’t always pretty, but the Buffalo Bills have escaped Sin City with a victory, defeating the Las Vegas Raiders 33-30 in a hard-fought contest. The Raiders put up a fight against our Bills, but ultimately, it was one turnover that made the difference, and fortunately for the Bills, it was forced by the guys in white and royal blue. The next time we’ll have Buffalo football to discuss will be in November, as the Bills head into their bye week next week sitting stop the AFC East Division with a 5-1 record. Our horns up and horns down for Buffalo’s final October contest are below. _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Down: C.J. Gardner-Johnson It wasn’t enough to miss tackles today. Gardner-Johnson outdid himself even beyond a poor performance by spitting at Raiders center Tyler Linderbaum, or tight end Brock Bowers, or just in the vicinity of the Raiders’ huddle. That led immediately to his ejection while Las Vegas was driving inside the two-minute warning towards the end of the first half. Gardner-Johnson is an edgy player, and he’s definitely shown that edge so far this season. While he’s arguably been their best safety, allowing just 10 of 18 passes to be completed when he’s the closest man in coverage, he’s struggled to wrap and tackle. Pro Football Reference credits him with six missed tackles already this season. I assume he’ll be suspended at least for Buffalo’s matchup with the Baltimore Ravens in two weeks, and deservedly so. That was an idiotic decision that put the team in a bad spot today. As a veteran, Gardner-Johnson needs to be better than doing something so stupid. He had one tackle before the ejection. Horns Up: Keon Coleman Every time quarterback Josh Allen needed a catch, he found No. 0. Coleman has continued to show growth this season, displaying good burst off the line of scrimmage, and sharpening his breaks in his routes. Coleman’s hands are great, as well, and he made some nice contested catches in addition to those where he was wide open. Coleman caught a wild touchdown pass in the third quarter on a quintessential Josh Allen ad-lib. That was the 258th touchdown pass of Allen’s career, which tied Hall of Fame quarterback Jim Kelly for the most in Bills history. Coleman might not be a Tee Higgins-like superstar, but he’s come along nicely in his third professional season. He finished with four catches for 59 yards and a score on six targets. Horns Up: Dorian Williams The inside linebacker made a play, intercepting Kirk Cousins in the third quarter. It looked like Williams was in zone while his closest defensive counterparts were in man, and when tight end Brock Bowers broke for an out route, Cousins expected Williams to follow suit. Instead, Williams sat in the middle of the field, and he was in position to intercept what would have otherwise been a completion to tight end Michael Mayer. Williams has struggled in coverage throughout his career, and he ceded some snaps in obvious passing downs to rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr today, but he was the guy who made a big play when the defense needed one. Williams finished the day with STATS in addition to the interception. Horns Up: Christian Benford The Bills’ top corner traveled for most of the game with the Raiders’ top receiving threat, tight end Brock Bowers. That’s no easy task for any defensive back, let alone a cornerback, but Benford was more than game for the assignment. He held Bowers in check throughout the night, as he didn’t even see his first target of the game until the third quarter. Entering the fourth quarter, Bowers had just two catches for 23 yards, and that was mostly due to Benford’s tight coverage. Did the defensive game plan leave more space for Vegas’ other tight end, Michael Mayer, to have a big game? It sure did. However, it was nice to watch the Bills have a clear plan to force someone other than a team’s best player beat them. Kudos to defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard for the design, but at the end of the day, players play. Inexplicably, the Bills went away from it for a few plays late in the game, and Bowers promptly burned them for two catches and 47 yards on consecutive plays. Benford was outstanding today despite being the closest in coverage to Tre Tucker on a fourth-quarter touchdown. Horns Down: Run Blocking Leading up to this one, the mismatch—at least on paper—seemed to be Buffalo’s offensive line vs. the run defense of the Raiders. Well, score one for the old cliche, because this is yet another example of why the games aren’t played on paper. James Cook III, who made a concerted effort to hang onto the football all day long, was able to find room to run, but it wasn’t an explosive-heavy day for him. Cook averaged right around four yards per carry, which would be fine for most running backs, but for a player averaging 5.6 yards per rush entering play, it wasn’t quite the day we expected, as the Bills averaged just 4.1 yards per rush on the game as a team when accounting for Josh Allen’s kneel-downs at the end of the game. Horns Up: Josh Allen The Western Time Zone is good to Allen, and today was another example. Even without DJ Moore, who was inactive today, Allen was able to buy time, find space, and make plays. The Raiders did well to keep him in the pocket, and even when Allen was able to escape, they prevented him from running wild like the Los Angeles Rams allowed him to do last week. Allen threw two touchdown passes—one to Khalil Shakir in the second quarter and another on the aforementioned ad-lib to Coleman—and showed patience even against solid Vegas coverage. Allen used his legs to keep plays alive so that he could find open receivers. The Raiders beat him up today, too, as he took some big shots throughout play. Allen finished 23-of-33 for 255 yards with two passing touchdowns and zero turnovers. He had just one yard rushing on five carries, though three of those “carries” we’re kneel-downs at the end of the game. Horns Up: Dalton Kincaid He didn’t gain much in the way of yardage, but Kincaid was active throughout this one. He saw a team-high eight targets and parlayed that into a team-high seven receptions. He had just 38 yards receiving, but his line would have looked much better had a touchdown catch in the third quarter n0t been wiped out by a holding penalty on O’Cyrus Torrence. Kincaid left briefly to have an x-ray on his ribs, but he returned to the game. It was nice to see him back as a focal point of the offense. Horns Up: James Cook III What a week for Buffalo’s top running back, who not only led the team in rushing yards, but also nearly led the team in receiving yards this week. After spending far too much time discussing ball security this week as it relates to Cook, it was nice to watch him dominate and protect the football. Cook is an elite player, and he put his mark on the proceedings tonight. He caught three passes for 58 yards, and his last reception looked like it was going to be a touchdown. Instead, he finished that scoring drive with a three-yard rushing touchdown to put the Bills on top for good. Cook finished with 22 carries for 95 yards and a score in addition to the three catches for 58 yards through the air. Horns Down: Pass Rush While the defensive secondary looked pretty solid overall today—Davison Igbinosun had three pass breakups, Maxwell Hairston made some plays, and rookie Jalon Kilgore even had a breakup in the fourth quarter—but they gave veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins plenty of time to feel comfortable in the pocket throughout the day. Cousins threw two fourth-quarter touchdown passes where, truthfully, the coverage couldn’t have been much better, but the veteran just put the ball in…

Perhaps the Bills have another thriller in store for fans this afternoon. title: Starkly split opinions on Buffalo Bills entering Week 6’s game at Raiders
summary: Life is all about perspective. So is football. How you view the Buffalo Bills right now is almost completely dependent on your natural outlook. They’re owners of the most explosive offense in the league. They’re averaging the most points per game. Josh Allen is the MVP favorite. James Cook is averaging 5.6 yards per carry. […]
full_text: Life is all about perspective. So is football. How you view the Buffalo Bills right now is almost completely dependent on your natural outlook. They’re owners of the most explosive offense in the league. They’re averaging the most points per game. Josh Allen is the MVP favorite. James Cook is averaging 5.6 yards per carry. Greg Rousseau is having an All-Pro caliber season. Deone Walker looks destined for future All-Pro distinctions himself. But they’re allowing the fifth-most points per game. The third-most yards. They have a -4 turnover differential. Their young cornerbacks have mostly struggled on the outside. The Bills are 4-1. But opinions of them feel extremely divided. Last week, on the Bills postgame radio show I host, six of the eight callers had negative takes on the air. After THAT victory over the Rams. The object of these games is to win them. Yet the collectively raised intelligence of football fans and media today can very easily understand that living dangerously can’t be sustained across a long, arduous season in the NFL or, especially, in the playoffs when all contests comes against quality opponents. I know teams aren’t exactly what their record says they are. That’s silly. But I happen to be a glass half full kind of guy. Did nature or nurture provide me that outlook? Probably a little of both. Even if you view the glass as half empty, that’s fine. There’s no right outlook. At this point of the season, I view the Bills as a team still trying to find itself. Most of that identity-searching is on the defensive side of course, but the passing offense hasn’t been right since Week 2, and DJ Moore being in and out of the lineup probably has much to do with that. Many teams are still looking to find themselves and by mid-October are 0-5, 1-4, or 2-3. With how incredibly thin margins between wins and losses have gotten in the modern-day NFL, clubs can’t apologize nor feel shameful about a winning record. These Bills certainly shouldn’t. There’s simultaneously plenty to rave about right now and clear flaws that need to be corrected. I don’t necessarily believe the Bills offense will continue to be as extravagantly awesome as it’s been through these first five games, although the presence of Allen strongly suggests Buffalo’s offense will be one of the league’s best. I don’t necessarily believe Cook will stay on an 1,800-yard pace. Early-season on-pace figures are pretty silly too. I don’t think he’ll continue to fumble at more than twice the league average either. And I don’t think the Bills defense, five games into the Jim Leonhard era, will continue to be as porous against the pass as it’s been to date. There are too many youngsters learning a brand-new defense for me to believe they won’t get better with time and on-field experience. Maybe you feel differently. And it’s fine if you do. But the Bills can help the strange split among fans and media regarding just how good this team is, or how sustainable its current dynamic is, today in Las Vegas. Now, do I think a convincing victory over the Raiders would persuade all those who don’t believe the Bills are very good that they indeed are? Probably not . What I do know about a Bills win today — it’d move them to 5-1, and they’d enter the bye week in one of the prime positions for the No. 1 seed in the AFC playoffs, which, to me, is the ultimate goal of the regular season. And, at 5-1, I’d say this Bills team would be pretty damn good.

title: The Optimist: An ugly win is still a win
summary: I don’t remember the last time the Carolina Panthers played a game this ugly and won. The final 25-14 score belies the fact that it was a one possession game deep in the fourth quarter. A bad snap on 1st & 10 for the Eagles and followed by the secondary losing Tommy Tremble for a […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Devin Lloyd #55 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates with teammate Lee Hunter #92 after a sack against the Philadelphia Eagles during the third quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images I don’t remember the last time the Carolina Panthers played a game this ugly and won. The final 25-14 score belies the fact that it was a one possession game deep in the fourth quarter. A bad snap on 1st & 10 for the Eagles and followed by the secondary losing Tommy Tremble for a 19-yard touchdown pass just seven plays later decided the game with 6:38 seconds left. In the end, the Panthers’ depleted defense barely managed to hold on against an even more depleted Philadelphia Eagles offense. Their offense played a worse game with Taylor Moton and Jalen Coker back on the field than they did against the Detroit Lions without either of them. Bryce Young was fine, but far from the cool, collected star against pressure that he has been most of the season. Ultimately, this is a team with many, well exposed flaws that is sitting at 3-2 with a division game against a reeling Tampa Bay Buccaneers squad next week that could turn their sole lead in the division into an awkward tie with the Saints or a commanding lead. It wasn’t a perfect win, but it was a win. Historically, the Panthers had to be absolutely perfect to win games. This is a trend that dates back to the early days of Cam Newton playing under Ron Rivera’s stifling conservative philosophies, continued through Matt Rhule’s managerial malpractices, and into the early days of Young’s hit and extremely miss young career. Often it felt like a single sack in the first quarter was enough to call the game a loss. Poor play at the start of a game would lead to pushing, which would lead to an interception, which would lead to chasing points, chasing yards, and then chasing air. None of that happened yesterday, in spite of a first quarter sack that derailed the Panthers second drive of the game. Coupled with all of the penalties, things could have been a lot worse. The #Panthers have set a new franchise for penalty yards in a game (144). Previous high was 120 against the Bucs in Week 2 of 2003. — Mike Kaye (@mike_e_kaye) October 18, 2026 The team floundered against the best defense they have faced all season, sure, but they never gave up, Young never turned the ball over, and the team still scored 25 points. Five things stand out to me about that score: It likely would have been another 30+ point game, but they decided to kneel out the clock from 1st and goal. They scored more than 25 points exactly once in 2023. They scored more than 25 points four times in 2024. They scored more than 25 points five times in 2025 They have scored 25 or more points in four out of five games so far in 2026. The offense still has a lot of wrinkles to either mix in or iron out, depending on your metaphor of choice, but they undeniably showed up against a good Eagles defense. My only real worry about them, ongoing health aside, is their ability to win in short yardage situations. That will be a problem that will haunt them down the stretch if they end up in the playoffs. The defensive secondary is still significantly undermanned. Not much they can or will do about that at this point in the season. Either the depth steps up while praying for Mike Jackson to return from his unspecified groin injury or it doesn’t. Jackson and Jaycee Horn have both missed two of their required four games while on injured reserve. Horn is not expected back as soon as that limit has been reached, but the word is still out on Jackson. For now, let’s enjoy both wins from yesterday. That’s right, I’m counting yesterday twice and for two good reasons. The first shows up obviously in the standings. 3-2 is a big accomplishment given where this team came from. They haven’t been 3-2 and arguably trending upwards since 2018, Rivera’s last full season as head coach. This could be a flash in the pan or it could be the start of something. The biggest thing supporting the latter is the second victory, confirmation of which will need to wait until the first injury report. For now, I’ll cross my fingers as I say that the Panthers escaped Philadelphia with both a win and no new names to add to their injured reserve list. You really couldn’t ask for a better Sunday.

full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - JANUARY 3: Bucky Irving #7 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers runs with the ball during the fourth quarter against the Carolina Panthers at Raymond James Stadium on January 3, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 3-2 Carolina Panthers open against the 1-5 Tampa Bay Buccaneers as favorites for only the second time this season and the first time since their road loss to the Cleveland Browns in Week 3. Week 7 Spread Panthers: -3 (-118) Buccaneers: +3 (-104) O/U 44.5 (-110/-110) Moneyline Panthers: -168 Buccaneers: +142 Remember that home-field advantage is traditionally accounted for by spotting the home team—the Panthers, in this case—three points on the spread. Questions abound as to who will start at quarterback for the Bucs against the Panthers—Daniels or Baker Mayfield. Either way, the Panthers young secondary will likely show some more growing pains. title: Panthers vs Eagles: Recap and analysis
summary: The Carolina Panthers played through a referee show to pull off a road win over the depleted Philadelphia Eagles, 25-14. First Quarter The Panthers defense was on the field first and got off to a strong start. Bobby Okereke sacked Tanner McKee on the first play and then nearly intercepted him on the second. The […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Tommy Tremble #82 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates his touchdown with Jalen Coker #18 against the Philadelphia Eagles in the second quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers played through a referee show to pull off a road win over the depleted Philadelphia Eagles, 25-14. First Quarter The Panthers defense was on the field first and got off to a strong start. Bobby Okereke sacked Tanner McKee on the first play and then nearly intercepted him on the second. The Eagles punted away, and a strong return by Trevor Etienne in his return set the Panthers up with good field position. Chuba Hubbard picked up a first down with his first carry, then Bryce Young hit Tetairoa McMillan a couple times to quickly move into field goal range. The drive stalled out and Dave Canales elected to kick a field goal on 4th and 4 seemingly anticipating a defensive struggle. Both teams exchanged a couple of ineffective drives that ended in punts. The quarter ended with the Eagles…I guess you could call it “driving” on the own side of their field. Second Quarter That drive almost moved when Tanner McKee completed an intermediate pass to DeVonta Smith, but it was called back for a holding in the backfield. That drive also ended a punt. Young completed a couple of passes to Jalen Coker to move the Panthers into Eagles territory. It looked like they had another big play to Mitchell Evans, but it was called back for a very inconsequential ineligible player down field call on Robert Hunt. A couple incompletions later, another punt. The defense forced another punt, and the punt was tipped and went out of bounds at the 35 yard line. The offense responded by picking up a first down via an Eagles penalty. On the next play, Young was not called for an intentional grounding (twice), and then after some complaining, the officials discussed and changed their mind and threw a flag like three minutes later. Young responded by completing a pass to McMillan while benefiting from a roughing the passer penalty going the other way. On the next play, Young found Tommy Tremble wide open in the flat and he took it to the end zone to put the Panthers up 10-0. The Eagles responded with a solid drive of their own. They were aided by a catch on what should have been an incomplete pass, but Dave Canales wasn’t able to get the challenge flag out quick enough. Two plays later, Will Lee was called for a phantom pass interference in the end zone. Another two plays later, Dameon Pierce punched it in. David Moore returned the kickoff out to midfield, but nothing eventful could happen in this game without a flag. The return was called back for a hold. On the next play, Chuba Hubbard’s nice run was called back for a hold. On the next play, the Panthers were called for ineligible players down field, but that one was declined. Young found Tetairoa McMillan to pick up a first down either way. Dave Canales turtled from there and elected to let the clock run out. Neither team called any timeouts, and the game went into the half with the Panthers holding a 10-7 lead. Third Quarter The Panthers picked up a couple of first downs on the first drive. One needed a Canales challenge to get the spot moved to a first down. The offense couldn’t muster more than that, but they did give Ryan Fitzgerald a chance to convert a 52 yard field goal to put the visitors up 13-7. The defense held the Eagles to another punt, but the offense stalled out around midfield once again. Devin Lloyd sacked Tanner McKee on the Eagles next possession while Will Lee had a couple of really nice coverage reps against DeVonta Smith to force yet another punt. The Panthers got backed into the shadow of the end zone, but Young found Jalen Coker breaking free in the middle of the field, and he scooted away for a 32 yard gain. Coker picked up another decent gain later in the drive, and Chuba Hubbard had a few hard runs. One of those came on a 4th and 1 to extend the drive into the fourth quarter. Fourth Quarter Young scrambled to the two yard line to bring up another 4th and 1. The offense stayed on the field, and Young was able to get them to jump on a hard count. Two plays later, Hubbard strolled off the left side for a touchdown. The offense stayed on the field for a 2-point conversion, but Young’s pass was knocked away. The Panthers eased off defensively, and that gave Tanner McKee the space to orchestrate a long drive without taking too much time. Devonta Smith briefly left the game after a hard fall, but he returned to catch a long touchdown over Will Lee. The Panthers bungled the kickoff and ended up deep in their own territory. The offense did nothing, then Sam Martin botched the punt. It looked like things were unraveling for Carolina, but the Eagles came to the rescue. A bad snap on first down put the Eagles way behind the sticks. The defense forced a punt, and Anthony Tyus broke through the line to block the punt. The offense finally took advantage of the field position. They picked up a first down with a Hubbard run, and an unnecessary roughness penalty tacked on more yardage. On the next play, Young found Tommy Tremble completely uncovered down the field for a touchdown. Tremble was called for taunting because he had the audacity to point in the general direction of an Eagles player. Ryan Fitzgerald missed the long extra point. The Panthers defense let the Eagles start moving the ball again, but Ejiro Evero dialed up the pressure when the Eagles got to midfield. Tre’von Moehrig notched a sack. On fourth down, McKee launched a jump ball to Smith, but Zaire Wheatley was able to range over and break up the pass. Chuba Hubbard grinded out a first down then David Moore took a bubble screen 27 yards inside the 15 yard line. One more first down run from Hubbard iced the game. Overview It was far from pretty, but a win is a win. The Panthers set a franchise record for penalty yardage in a game (149) but were able to overcome that and put up a solid 25 points against a vaunted Eagles defense. Chuba Hubbard had an admirable workhorse performance with 28 carries for 120 yards, and Bryce Young put together a quiet 281 yards passing, even if the completion percentage wasn’t great. On defense, Will Lee IV did a very good job on DeVonta Smith, who was basically the only offensive weapon the Eagles had left. The group did what they should have done against an opponent with a makeshift offensive line and dearth of play makers. They limited the Eagles to just 3.6 yards per play. The penalties are really the only thing that kept the Eagles in the game. The Panthers move to 3-2 with the win. They’ll try to keep that momentum going when they host the division rival Buccaneers next Sunday.

title: Panthers fans optimistic, in spite of short term concerns
summary: Fans of the Carolina Panthers have a lot of bright side to look at these days, even though their favorite team’s list of injuries is rivaled only by this week’s opponent. Carolina is 2-2, coming back healthier from their early bye week, and managed to hold onto the lead in the NFC South despite not […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Jaycee Horn #8 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates during an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fans of the Carolina Panthers have a lot of bright side to look at these days, even though their favorite team’s list of injuries is rivaled only by this week’s opponent. Carolina is 2-2, coming back healthier from their early bye week, and managed to hold onto the lead in the NFC South despite not playing in Week 5. Bryce Young is playing the best ball of his career. Devin Lloyd looks like the free agent signing of the century when he’s healthy. Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker, when healthy, are feasting under Young’s newfound confidence and competence. Really, what’s not to love? 88% of Panthers fans are confident in the current direction of the franchise. That is in line with the high numbers that our Reacts surveys have been returning for most of the season. These are amazing numbers for a franchise that everybody thought had a decent chance of picking near the top of the 2027 NFL Draft. If I told you at the during the 2026 NFL Draft that, by the bye week, Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, Jonathon Brooks, Brady Christensen, Taylor Moton, Ikem Ekwonu, Nic Scourton, Tershawn Wharton, and Xavier Legette would all be injured reserve already, then you would have likely and reasonably assumed the Panthers were already at 0-4 and looking to sell off their used parts for pennies on the dollars. Instead, the team is somehow trending upwards in spite of only returning Moton and Wharton off of that list in the week after the bye. There are legitimate concerns about the status and future of this roster. No team is going to lose both of their starting outside corners and thrive afterwards. The Panthers are fortunate that their next major test is Philadelphia Eagles backup quarterback Tanner McKee. With most of his receivers having missed significant practice time—if they are even all playing on Sunday—the odds of him being the centered of a well-oiled passing machine are low. What actually happens next is anybody’s guess, but Panthers fans have to be feeling pretty good about their chances today. Checkout FanDuel , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation.

title: Bears’ Kyler Gordon was ‘Confident’ and ‘Absolutely’ ready to play
summary: That was a historic season debut by defensive back Kyler Gordon in the Chicago Bears’ 31 to 23 win over the Atlanta Falcons. Gordon had 4 tackles, 3 tackles for loss, 3 sacks, and 2 forced fumbles. His 3 sacks tie the NFL record for sacks by a defensive back in a game, and it’s […]
full_text: Oct 18, 2026; Atlanta, Georgia, USA; Chicago Bears defensive back Kyler Gordon (6) strips the ball from Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. (9) during the third quarter at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brett Davis-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect That was a historic season debut by defensive back Kyler Gordon in the Chicago Bears’ 31 to 23 win over the Atlanta Falcons. Gordon had 4 tackles, 3 tackles for loss, 3 sacks, and 2 forced fumbles. His 3 sacks tie the NFL record for sacks by a defensive back in a game, and it’s the first time a Bear has done it since Todd Bell in 1983. He did his damage in only 16 defensive snaps, which is the fewest snaps a player with 3 or more sacks in a game has played in the past 20 seasons. Gordon’s 21-day practice window had him practice in full for all 9 practices he attended, but you can’t truly replicate in-game conditioning without playing, which is why Gordon was on a pitch count today. The Bears could have waited until his window expired next week, but the Bears wanted him back, and Gordon wanted to be back. Bears’ head coach Ben Johnson was asked about Gordon’s performance at his postgame press conference. “He was ready to play,” Johnson said. “I talked with Kyler yesterday morning and said, ‘Hey, I think we want to activate you. Are you ready to go?’ And he said, ‘Absolutely.’ And he sure enough was. So, huge spark there for us on the defense. I thought DA (Dennis Allen) put him in some good spots, but I mean, he’s so twitchy. He’s very hard to block as a blitzer; tight in coverage also. So, you know, we got to make sure that we keep him on that right track. We’re trying to limit his role a little bit, just making sure he was in good football shape. But those snaps that he had were huge ones for us today.” Gordon also met the media after the game, and he seemed to let some frustration boil over (you can watch it below and come to your own conclusion) , but I get it. His head coach seemed irritated at times when asked about him in pressers. There was clearly a disconnect in the rehab the team wanted from him and the rehab he felt he needed. Some fans and media have questioned his desire to play for months, calling him soft and saying he’s faking it for a paycheck. Gordon opened his press conference with this line: “I wanted to be on the field and contribute and add to this team and help drive the direction where we’re going to go, and that’s what I did.” He was asked if he was on the same page with the Bears’ medical staff after his time away with his personal trainer, and he said that’s a “question for coach,” adding it’s not his call. They asked again about the rehab situation, and he reiterated he can’t answer, saying he is “more focused on what we got in the future.” Gordon talked about getting his conditioning right in the coming weeks, but as far as any hesitation in playing today, he said he was “confident” he was good to go. The Bears are better when Gordon is on the field, so let’s hope he stays out of the trainer’s room. In case you missed it, Gordon got a game ball from Johnson after the game, and it looked like something was said during the congratulatory hug. Needed this. pic.twitter.com/0lDzBSPmX3 — Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) October 18, 2026
