title: Keys before kickoff: Cowboys at Packers Week 6
summary: The 2-3 Dallas Cowboys travel to Lambeau Field to face the 3-2 Green Bay Packers this week on Sunday Night Football. Here are three keys to the game. Exploit Green Bay’s front With the weapons both of these teams possess on the outside, the signs point to this game being a shootout. But what if […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images The 2-3 Dallas Cowboys travel to Lambeau Field to face the 3-2 Green Bay Packers this week on Sunday Night Football . Here are three keys to the game. Exploit Green Bay’s front With the weapons both of these teams possess on the outside, the signs point to this game being a shootout. But what if it didn’t have to be? The Packers possess a lackluster run defense, ranking near the bottom of the league in run-stop metrics. They’re also dealing with injuries at defensive tackle and linebacker. This week in Lambeau could provide Brian Schottenheimer a chance to commit to running the ball with Javonte Williams, should he so choose. If Dallas is able to establish themselves on the ground and remain balanced, that’ll help keep the dangerous Green Bay passing attack on the sideline. Long, clock-chewing drives are one of the paths to victory for the Cowboys. But this team will need to make some changes for this to be effective. Mainly, the play-caller cannot abandon the ground game. There has to be a clear dedication to successfully moving the ball with Williams on the ground behind the offensive line. Dallas has shown the ability when they choose to do so. We should also see some subtle and not-so-subtle personnel adjustments this week, according to coach Schottenheimer, via Tommy Yarrish : “I’m not going to get to a bunch of them. Obviously, there’s a competitive advantage. But there’ll be some roster adjustments you guys will see. Some will be more noticeable than others, and some will be subtle as you look at it.” Could this mean more Brevyn Spann-Ford and less Jake Ferguson at tight end in 11 personnel? Ferguson has not been a serviceable blocker and he’s averaging just 20 yards on three receptions per game. Unfortunately, he just has not given this team enough in 2026. Meanwhile, Spann-Ford is an extremely physical player with the willingness and ability to take on edges and linebackers. This could be the week we see his snap count begin to increase if Dallas truly is committed to running the ball. Defuse Green Bay’s explosives The Packers run game has not been effective. And the team had not scored much before their coming out party against the Bears last week, averaging just 18.25 points per game in weeks one through four. So what makes this Packers offense so dangerous? One word: explosives. Last week, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden broke free against the Bears secondary, posting totals of 143 and 123 yards respectively. Their longest catches of the day went for 53 and 50 yards. Even tight end Tucker Craft snagged a 46-yard catch downfield. According to SumerSports, this Packers offense threw the ball deep on 22.6% of their plays last week. If the deep ball is there, Jordan Love will take it. So how does Dallas prevent the explosive plays? Given what we’ve seen this season, it’ll be a tough task. But there are ways. The arrival of Joey Porter Jr. unlocks new doors for Christian Parker on defense, as long as he plays (questionable with an ankle). He now has a player that he should be able to completely trust in tight man coverage. This allows Parker to be more aggressive with his players around the line of scrimmage. With the Dallas four-man rush being one of the league’s worst in taking down opposing quarterbacks, expect to see more pass blitzes and five-man fronts moving forward. As we saw from Tampa Bay last week, getting to a quarterback is the best way to shut down an explosive passing game. Consistently pressuring Love needs to be a major focus this week for the Cowboys defense. Dallas needs to force the Packers into third-and-long throughout the game, given the weakness of Green Bay’s rushing attack. When they get into this down and distance, it’s imperative they get off the field. Mistakes such as blown coverages and turf monster induced slips must be limited. One of the most frustrating facets of the Cowboys defense to watch this season has been the 22 yards gains on 3rd and 21. Without mental mistakes on defense, that down and distance is nearly impossible to convert. Tighten up in these situations and get off the field. The last way to limit Green Bay’s explosives has nothing to do with the defense. As mentioned in the first key, keeping your own offense on the field with long, methodical drives is a great way to shorten the game. But those drives also need to end in touchdowns, not field goals. It is actually detrimental to consume that much clock just to put up three. Long drives on offense ending in touchdowns might just be the most important key to a win this week. Attacking the blitz On average, one out of three defensive play calls from Green Bay is some sort of blitz. That’s not an exceedingly high number when compared to the rest of the league (ranked 12th in blitz percentage) but it is noteable when considering how Tampa Bay was able to fluster Dak Prescott and the Cowboys offense with a barrage of blitzes last week. I’m not a big believer in blueprints because everyone’s personnel is different, but this could be a week where the Packers try and somewhat emulate what the Buccaneers did to the Cowboys offense. If the Packers do travel that dangerous, heavy-blitz road, Prescott will need to diagnose pre-snap and get the ball out quickly. The Cowboys took far too long last week to get their slant game going with George Pickens to defeat Tampa Bay’s pass rush. This week, the short passing game with in-breaking routes needs to be a focus if they’re facing an onslaught of blitzes. If they’re able to beat the Packers extra men early, Green Bay should back off. Dallas can also beat a blitz-heavy assault on the ground. That double-edged sword can bite the blitzing team if the runner is able to get past the extra men and into the second level. Blitzing into the incorrect gap leaves plenty of room for the offensive line to clear a path for Williams and the other backs. On top of that, the Packers have already shown a weakness in run defense. And once that ground game is established, things should open up downfield off of play action. The formula is clear, but execution is what matters.

title: 3 under-the-radar players for Cowboys at Packers
summary: After a 2-3 record through five weeks, the Dallas Cowboys desperately need a win as they look for answers to what went wrong. The offense has top-three potential, but the loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers showed it needs near-perfection to win. It wasn’t considered possible, but the defense has taken a step back from […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images After a 2-3 record through five weeks, the Dallas Cowboys desperately need a win as they look for answers to what went wrong. The offense has top-three potential, but the loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers showed it needs near-perfection to win. It wasn’t considered possible, but the defense has taken a step back from where it was last year under Matt Eberflus. Now they travel to Green Bay to face a Packers team in a similar spot to Dallas, performing below expectations, but coming off a convincing, almost get-right game against their division rival, the Chicago Bears. After early-season struggles, Jordan Love has found his footing and should push the ball downfield with wide receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden. The Cowboys will need all hands on deck, but three players could fly under the radar and swing the game if Dallas wants to leave Lambeau Field with its first win in the Dak Prescott era since the regular-season win in 2016. Tyler Goodson Cowboys offensive coordinator Klayton Adams said they need to give Tyler Goodson more touches on offense this week. In the last two weeks, the Cowboys RB2 has had just three carries. He had zero attempts in the loss to Tampa Bay. When Dallas acquired Goodson, he showed some really good things against the Baltimore Ravens. Since then, the offense has relied too much on Javonte Williams to be both the power and speed back in the run game. Unfortunately, speed isn’t what Williams is best at. Facing a Green Bay Packers pass defense that ranks fourth-best in EPA per pass play and 19th in EPA per rush, Dallas has to run the ball well this weekend to get the offense going. Goodson has done everything so far to show he’s earned more carries in the role carved out for Malik Davis. Against Green Bay, we should see him more in the screen game and have more explosive runs. Ryan Flournoy Similar to Goodson at running back, Ryan Flournoy could be in for his best game of the season. As mentioned above, the Packers have a really good pass defense. The unit gives up 6.4 pass yards per pass attempt, tied for eighth best with the Denver Broncos. That means they aren’t giving up explosive passes like Dallas’ defense does. Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has plenty of experience facing Dak Prescott, and with a lot of success. His last two matchups with the Arizona Cardinals have been some of his worst. Gannon will try to take away not just one of CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, but both. That means Flournoy will have some one-on-one matchups that he’ll have to win. Flournoy’s best statistical game of the season came against Tampa Bay with three receptions for 90 yards. Given the looks he’ll get, this could be a game where he ends up with eight targets, seven receptions, and just over 100 yards. Flournoy hasn’t caught a touchdown pass this year, so let’s throw one in there for him too. Bryan Anger Nothing’s more under the radar than an NFL team’s punter. Bryan Anger hasn’t had to do much so far in five weeks. Entering Sunday, Anger will have punted only ten times. That ties Buffalo Bills punter Tommy Doman Jr. for the fewest punts in the NFL. That’s a credit to Dallas’ efficient offense. Anger could matter more in this game because the Packers’ defense could limit the Cowboys’ passing attack, their bread and butter all season. If Dallas can’t get their running game going, we’ll see a lot more of Anger punting the ball away. Pinning the Green Bay Packers offense deep in their own territory should ease the pressure on Dallas’ defense to work through its issues. Anger averages 49.6 yards per punt this year, tied for seventh best among punters, so more than enough leg to flip the field. Dallas will win this game by staying efficient on offense while building momentum on defense. If Anger can pin the Packers inside their 20 for most of the game, that should set the defense up much better so their backs aren’t against the wall and Green Bay can run up the scoreboard.

title: Cowboys at Packers: 2 players to buy, and 2 to sell
summary: The Dallas Cowboys are heading to Green Bay for a Week 6 matchup with plenty of questions to answer after their disappointing 24-16 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The offense has shown it can put up points, but turnovers and missed opportunities continue to get in the way, while the defense is still struggling […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys are heading to Green Bay for a Week 6 matchup with plenty of questions to answer after their disappointing 24-16 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The offense has shown it can put up points, but turnovers and missed opportunities continue to get in the way, while the defense is still struggling to make the plays that can change a game. Here are two players to buy and two to sell heading into Sunday’s matchup with the Packers. Buy: WR George Pickens George Pickens finally delivered the kind of performance Cowboys fans have been waiting for, and Dallas needs to keep him involved as it heads into a difficult road matchup. Against Tampa Bay, Pickens caught nine of 13 targets for 130 yards and a touchdown, giving him his best receiving performance of the season. His 18-yard touchdown reception in the fourth quarter also gave Dallas a chance to make things interesting late in the game. It was a strong response after a solid outing against Houston, when he caught two passes for 75 yards. Through five games, Pickens has recorded 27 receptions for 355 yards and a touchdown, averaging 13.2 yards per catch. Those numbers leave a little to be desired, but his most recent performance showed what he can provide when Dak Prescott consistently looks his way. On top of that, all the defensive penalties he’s drawn have helped the Cowboys move the chains. The key is making sure last week’s performance becomes a trend rather than a one-game spike. Pickens has shown he can be a difference-maker, and the Cowboys should continue giving him the targets to prove it. Sell: DaRon Bland (and the defensive secondary) Before last week’s disaster, the thinking was that the Cowboys’ secondary would eventually start making plays. That point, however, may continue to elude this secondary. Through five games, Dallas has zero interceptions, the worst possible number in a category that can change the direction of an entire game. The lack of takeaways is especially frustrating because this defense has had opportunities. Against Tampa Bay, DaRon Bland nearly redeemed a difficult night when he got his hands on a pass from rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels, only to drop a potential pick-six interception. Bland also committed costly penalties and even slipped in coverage at one point, allowing a huge play. Bland’s struggles are becoming increasingly difficult to overlook. He has built a reputation as a playmaker, but the Cowboys need more than reputation right now. They need sound coverage, fewer costly penalties and, most importantly, interceptions. Bland and the secondary have not delivered consistently enough in any of those areas. Joey Porter Jr.’s return gives Dallas another experienced cornerback option, but adding talent to the back end will only go so far if the pass rush cannot make quarterbacks uncomfortable. The Cowboys have recorded just five sacks through five games. When quarterbacks have time to survey the field, even capable defensive backs can be left covering receivers for too long. That is the larger issue: the secondary has not created turnovers, but it is also being asked to hold up while the pass rush struggles to generate consistent pressure against an explosive passing game. Dallas needs both units to improve. Until the defensive backs start turning opportunities into takeaways and the front creates more disruption, it is hard to trust this group against a Green Bay offense led by Jordan Love and featuring big-play receivers like Christian Watson. Buy: Javonte Williams Javonte Williams has been productive enough this season to deserve more opportunities, especially when Dallas gets inside the red zone. The Cowboys have leaned on him at times, but his workload should be a bigger part of the offensive plan against Green Bay. Williams has carried the ball 74 times for 276 yards and six rushing touchdowns through five games, averaging 3.7 yards per carry. He has also contributed 17 receptions for 94 yards and a receiving touchdown. The rushing average is hardly eye-popping, but the touchdown production is difficult to overlook: Williams has consistently been a useful option when Dallas needs to finish a drive. He scored Dallas’ opening touchdown against Tampa Bay, punching in a one-yard run to cap the Cowboys’ first possession. He also broke off a 21-yard gain earlier in the drive, showing he can contribute beyond short-yardage situations. The opportunity here is about balance. Dallas has relied heavily on Prescott and the passing game, and while that can produce plenty of yardage, the offense becomes more predictable when the run game is an afterthought. Giving Williams more carries would help the Cowboys stay ahead of the chains, keep the defense honest and potentially create better play-action opportunities for Prescott and his receivers. Green Bay’s defense has been more effective at creating turnovers than Dallas’, but the Cowboys should still look for ways to test the Packers on the ground rather than asking Prescott to carry the offense on every important possession. Williams’ six rushing touchdowns demonstrate that he can be trusted in scoring situations. Dallas needs to give him a bigger role and see whether that production can translate into more consistent success between the 20s. Sell: Jake Ferguson Jake Ferguson keeps landing on this list for all the wrong reasons. Ferguson’s performance against Tampa Bay was the kind that can change how a team evaluates a player’s role. The tight end finished with three catches for 19 yards on six targets, and two of his drops included the night’s most damaging play: a late-game mistake that turned a potential comeback drive into a game-sealing interception. Ferguson also dropped a pass during Dallas’ two-minute drive before halftime, costing the offense an opportunity. The mistakes weren’t limited to one moment; a growing supply of film shows how much of a liability he has become in the blocking game. The concerns go beyond one game. Ferguson has not eclipsed 43 receiving yards in any of his first five games, and he has not provided the consistent production Dallas needs from a starting tight end. His value is not measured only by catches and yards; he also needs to be a dependable target in the middle of the field and help the offense convert important downs. Instead, his recent drops have become a major source of frustration. Ferguson has earned the opportunity to bounce back, but that does not mean the Cowboys should ignore what happened in Tampa Bay. Dallas needs dependable execution, particularly in high-leverage situations. After another costly performance, Ferguson has to prove he can regain the trust Prescott and the offense need from him.
author: Jorge Guajardo

title: Broncos vs. Seahawks: The No Bull Review
summary: We’re a finicky bunch here in Broncos Country. Also, the media is always a fickle bunch of knee-jerk creatures with little to no nuance for this game that we love.  Let me lay some No Bull truth down for you all that can hopefully talk some of you back from the ledge into wading into […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Kris Abrams-Draine #31 celebrates with Ja'Quan McMillian #29 of the Denver Broncos after securing an interception during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Empower Field at Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re a finicky bunch here in Broncos Country. Also, the media is always a fickle bunch of knee-jerk creatures with little to no nuance for this game that we love. Let me lay some No Bull truth down for you all that can hopefully talk some of you back from the ledge into wading into the abyss about Bo Nix and the offensive woes that Fitz-ception and the rest of the talking heads are freaking out about. Credit where it is due The #1 thing that everyone who’s trying to dump on Bo Nix right now is forgetting is that the Seattle Seahawks have an absolutely fierce defense that matches up VERY well against our offense. Their front is one of the best in the game. They schematically crush average run games (and let’s be honest, ours is not average: it is poor). They also make it extremely hard on the back end to complete deep passes. Everyone wants to talk about how bad Nix is, but has absolutely no clue about what happened on the film. I do not have access to All-22, but I can tell you there were NOT people open against that defense. When the broadcast did show us the better angles, our receivers were smothered outside of one singular play. Dial back the perspective a little wider. We just played 6 of the toughest defenses in the NFL, and our two losses came to two of the undefeated teams as it stands today: the 49ers and Chiefs. This game was never going to be pretty offensively. This 6-game stretch was never going to be roses and touchdowns. Perspective is needed Let’s be better fans and think a little deeper. We’ve seen so much of this story before. Bo Nix struggled just as badly last season, the same way early in the season. We looked terrible in a Thursday night game last season. This run game is a stinking hot one and a half-foot-wide cow patty, and our wide receivers are very much overrated and inconsistent. Thinking back a little further, I saw this same story back in the 2015 season. I think a lot of you have forgotten just how pathetic the offense was under Peyton Manning and Brock Osweiler that season. That team got dragged by the defense all the way to the Super Bowl. Take a deep breath, Broncos Country. Uncle Sadaraine is here to tell you this season is not in danger…it is actually just getting started. More on that when we wrap up. For now, let’s dig into reviewing this game. Offense While I love to see a coach dedicated to the run game, I am getting quite uncomfortable with how much we lean into a part of the game that performs so poorly. We ran into 8 and 9-man boxes (loosely…you could say the safety was out of the box, but he was only out by one friggin step) multiple times. I do not understand how this offense wasn’t dialing up a quick slant / out or a play-action audible more often. Either the players aren’t capable of adjusting on the field for whatever strange reason, or Payton doesn’t trust them to execute (or both). But we had many 2 and less yard gains because of running into stacked boxes with a back who looks completely washed and a line that is inconsistent at executing their blocks. Yes, we made 2 drives work with a run game that churned out production. But when that dried up, they just kept hitting the same buttons hoping for it to finally work. It was absolute insanity through the 3rd and 4th quarters. One problem I saw was a problem with design. In the 4th quarter on 3rd and 10, the play design was absolutely mind-boggling to the side Nix was reading. Both outside routes Nix was looking at were in-breaking next to each other with a safety over the top. There was no space for him to find a play to throw to. Just have those guys scissor and give your quarterback a read to throw to one-on-one. They can’t keep a safety over both if you do that. Quarterbacks Bo Nix is not broken. He has regressed this season at some level, but I do expect that at some level when his offseason was spent recovering from a broken ankle and 2nd surgery. I know Broncos Country is absolutely coo coo for Cocoa Puffs when it comes to quarterback play, but you all need to ease up. This is only his 3rd year, and he did NOT have a full offseason to sharpen his skill set. I’m not saying he’s a great quarterback. I think he’s looking average at best. But when we think about how many good defenses he’s been facing, I have to think there’s a really great opportunity in front of him to start rounding into form as the season wears on. I do get frustrated on 3rd down after 3rd down with him not producing something, but I’d love someone to show me all the opportunities he missed because they sure as hell didn’t look to me to be there when we did get coverage angles. Line This line had a good half with really well-executed blocks for two touchdown drives. As the game wore on, they wore down, and the play got choppy up front (especially in the run plays). They ran power a few times that were as good as you will see in the NFL this weekend. I was rather disappointed with Luke Wattenburgh’s bad snap. At what point will he play like a long-term starting center? Running Backs RJ Harvey is the one guy on the offense that is playing inspired football. He’s only getting a couple of handfuls of touches each game, but he’s making them count. He executed a great screen play with a great block from Wattenburg out in space for a 16-yard gain. Later on the same drive, he pulled off another to get the ball inside the 10. He also converted a 3rd and 1 out of shotgun by shooting to the outside. He took a wild cat snap to the house for the 2nd touchdown of the game. He finished with 6 runs for 25 yards (4.2 ypc) and 3 catches on 4 targets for 31 yards. We’re going to go way back with JK Dobbins to spit some No Bull truth this week. JK Dobbins is Lance Ball. He’s a guy we’re feeding who knows the offense but just doesn’t bring anything worthwhile to the table. His touchdown run was a credit to the line (one of their best blocked plays of the game). He had one good run for 16 yards where he actually jump-stepped to avoid a tackle for 16 yards. But he only created 41 yards on 17 carries (2.4 ypc). Without that one 16-yard run, he was 16 for 25, which is 1.57 ypc. This is honestly dog shit production from a running back. The SECOND that Jonah Coleman gets back, he should get a start over Dobbins or Tyler Badie. Dobbins is a detriment to this offense and should be treated as such. He’s supposed to be a power back who can power through tackles, and I just don’t see that in his game this year. Let’s throw in some credit to Tyler Badie for his big conversion on 4th and 3 behind Meinerz and McGlinchey. It was a shame he got injured and was out of the game, as I think he deserves more opportunities given what we’ve seen in front of him so far this season. Receivers None of our receivers are worthy of anything positive this week. They got owned by and large the whole game and did not create separation to give Nix options. Cortland Sutton dropped a pass that hit him in the hands. Jaylen Waddle got dinged up and finished the game, but was only 4 out of 7 targets for 24 yards. The receivers and tight ends were smothered by the Seahawks defense and did not find a way to fight that got them openings. Defense Vance Joseph and this defense deserve all the credit in the world for this win. They were a salient force that does not get enough credit for how well they have been playing. JSN is the Seahawks’ offense. He got his 134 yards on 12 receptions. I will take that all day, and I’m not even kidding. Vance had his guys play a mix of off coverage or press with a safety over the top and set things up so that JSN was never allowed to get a ton of space to work…

title: The Broncos keep finding ways to win, no matter the challenge
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! The Denver Broncos find ways to win games. Period. All of this nonsense on is this sustainable … it’s the makeup of this team. It was the case last season. It’s the case this season. You can call it moxie. You can call resiliency. In the end, the Broncos just find […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Head Coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos stands on the field prior to an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Empower Field at Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! The Denver Broncos find ways to win games. Period. All of this nonsense on is this sustainable … it’s the makeup of this team. It was the case last season. It’s the case this season. You can call it moxie. You can call resiliency. In the end, the Broncos just find a way to get victories. After the six-game gauntlet Denver had to start the season, sitting at 4-2 is a helluva feat. As Broncos head coach Sean Payton said after the 17-14 overtime win over the Seattle Seahawks: “Here’s what I said to them. There’s still, obviously, a lot of things that we can improve on, we have to. When this initial stretch was given to us, it’s hard to figure out in our league, you guys know that. When you look at last season, and then you project what teams are going to be like, it’s hard to do. We found a way to get four wins. “We understand that certainly we have to become more effective, more efficient offensively, and yet … Even in the kicking game, I thought we hit the huge field goal, but they won that battle tonight, they did relative to field position. Defense really was lights out. … It was a good win, but there’s a lot of work to do.” Yes, Bo Nix and the offense need to get better. But you would much rather sit at 4-2 with areas to improve upon rather than the alternative. “Shoot, we just have to execute,” Broncos running back J.K. Dobbins said to the media after the game. “You know, we’ve played some really good defenses. Every single team we’ve played has a really good defense. So you just got to go to the drawing board and figure it out and execute. That is what it comes down to, execution.” There’s also that added motivation to correct the issues and to know the offense is capable of more. “For sure. I think as we go, as we continue to go throughout the season, we’ll just find ways to get better and better,” Nix said. “I do think you have to (attribute it to) the schedule, just the first six games we knew were going to be tough. To come out 4-2 with really a complete team effort in all six games, it’s a complete team effort to get four of those wins. We came up short just barely in San Fran. We could be 5-1. 4-2 is a really good spot, and then as an offense, we’ll figure out ways to continue to improve.” In the end, all that matters is the Broncos are 4-2 after a brutal stretch to open the season. And as is the case with this team, it just finds ways to win games. “The record,” Payton said when asked what gives him reason to smile about the 4-2 record. “Meaning I say that the record, because those wins are hard to get. So we just played a real good team, and I feel like we can continue to improve. Being at 4-2 right at this little three-day stretch and then get ready next week, that’d be the honest … And again, I’m a little bit of a realist to know that four and two could easily be two and four.” Broncos links

full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 27: Jameson Williams #1 of the Detroit Lions scores a touchdown during the second quarter against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on November 27, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions (3-2) will host their division rival Green Bay Packers (4-2) in Week 7, and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -3.5 points . The Packers finished their 2025 season by snagging the seven seed in the playoffs, but the Bears eliminated them in the Wild Card round. Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley was hired to be the next head coach of the Miami Dolphins, and Green Bay hired Jonathan Gannon (previously the head coach of the Cardinals) as a replacement. With Gannon came a new 3-4 defense and a whole bunch of changes on the defensive side of the ball. EDGE Rashan Gary was traded to the Cowboys, NT Colby Wooden was traded to the Colts, while EDGE Kingsley Enagbare, MIKE Quay Walker, and CB Nate Hobbs departed in free agency. EDGE/LB Micah Parsons continues to recover from an ACL tear and is not expected to be available in Week 7. Being up against the cap, the Packers elected to promote from within, inserting EDGE Lukas Van Ness and ILB Isaiah McDuffie into the starting lineup, trading for LB Zaire Franklin (who is starting in place of injured Edgerrin Cooper), and drafting starters CB Brandon Cisse (second round) and NT Chris McClellan (third) on Day 2 of the NFL Draft. On offense, the Packers lost QB Malik Willis, RB Emanuel Wilson, WR Dontayvion Wicks (traded to the Eagles), WR Romeo Dobbs, LT Rasheed Walker, and LG/C Elgton Jenkins; like on defense, they elected to mostly promote from within, elevating RB Marshawn Lloyd into a bigger role (especially with Josh Jacobs suspended—he is expected to return in Week 7), WR Savion Williams and LT Jordan Morgan into the starting lineup, and shifting Sean Rhyan inside to center. Their guard spots have been a massive problem, and the Packers have been searching for answers, with their most recent pairing being RG Travis Glover and former Lion LG Laken Tomlinson (starting in place of the injured Aaron Banks). After a slow start to their 2026 season, the Packers have settled down as their offense has found its groove. The Packers opened the season with a loss after allowing the Vikings to drop 39 points on them, rebounded in Week 2 by beating the Jets by three points, only to lose again in Week 3 as the Falcons dominated them on the ground to the tune of 35 points. In Week 4, the Packers once again found a way to win by three points, this time over the Bucs, then smashed a Caleb Williams-less Bears team 31-7. In Week 6, the Packers took on the Cowboys’ 31st-ranked defense on “Sunday Night Football,” and while they jumped out to a 17-0 lead in the first half, they only scored six points in the second half. Fortunately, their defense held strong and allowed only 13 points, and the game ended in a 23-13 win. With the Packers offense in a groove, the Lions secondary is certainly going to be tested. Will they be able to carry over the success they had against the Cardinals in Week 5? Will Brian Branch return? If so, how big of a factor will he be? With so much unknown about the Lions’ defense, there’s a real chance the Packers continue their run of putting up points, and Detroit will need their top-scoring offense to keep pace and lead the Lions to victory. title: Discussion: Which Detroit Lions player needs to have a bigger impact post-bye?
summary: A winning football team is typically a well-oiled machine. While the Detroit Lions have won three games to start the 2026 season, there is still room to improve. Five games into the year, it has been a mixed bag for the Lions. The offense is humming, averaging almost 33 points per game. The defense is […]
full_text: A winning football team is typically a well-oiled machine. While the Detroit Lions have won three games to start the 2026 season, there is still room to improve. Five games into the year, it has been a mixed bag for the Lions. The offense is humming, averaging almost 33 points per game. The defense is not, allowing nearly 30 points per game. Those two numbers tell a story: the Lions are playing shootout-style football. That is not necessarily a bad thing, but we are nearing the extreme—the offense needs to be perfect, while the defense is scrounging for impactful plays. The Week 5 victory over the Arizona Cardinals was a much-needed turnaround, as both sides of the ball looked sharp. However, that performance needs to be a blueprint going forward, not an outlier. One way to make that happen is for Lions players to step up. Today’s Question of the Day is: Which Detroit Lions player needs to have a bigger impact post-bye? My answer : Jack Campbell. Unfortunately, there are a number of viable answers to this question. On offense, Jameson Williams (18 catches for 276 yards and two touchdowns) and Isaac TeSlaa (nine catches for 187 yards) are two names that immediately come to mind. For Williams, it would be nice to see more consistency, whether that means catching the football or being more impactful on intermediate plays. As for TeSlaa, it would be nice to see him more involved in general. Even with Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sam LaPorta, Jahmyr Gibbs, and Williams ahead of him on the depth chart, fewer than 10 receptions and zero touchdowns is a surprise for a player that appeared to be ascending this time last season. On defense, you could name anyone in the secondary. At cornerback, the Lions need more impactful play from D.J. Reed and whoever is CB2 for the week, whether it is Roger McCreary, Ennis Rakestraw, or Rock Ya-Sin. At safety, the Lions drastically need Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph back; the return of the former looks promising while the latter remains a question mark. However, my pick is Jack Campbell. The bar was set high after an impressive All-Pro campaign in 2025, but we have not seen that level from Campbell so far in 2026. Whereas Campbell was a football-seeking missile last season, he has been out of sorts far too often this season. The coverage has taken a serious nosedive, and he (and other Lions linebackers) have been targeted heavily. Given the struggles of the linebacking unit as a whole, I am inclined to believe that it might be a schematic issue rather than a talent issue. Regardless, Campbell is one of the most important parts of the Lions defense, and his play has simply not met expectations. For the Lions to have a successful post-bye stretch, they will need him to return to form. Which Lions player needs to step up in the coming weeks? Let us know in the comments below.

full_text: When Detroit Lions star defensive back Brian Branch returns to the field in the next few weeks, many around the team are hoping they will get the same player that everyone grew accustomed to seeing prior to him suffering an Achilles injury in December of 2025. However, Branch has also gone through a transformation during his long road back to the field, as Dan Pompei of The Athletic highlights in his latest profile piece: Anger consumed Brian Branch. Then the Lions star made a promise that changed everything . “Man, he’s a pit bull,” Lions coach Dan Campbell says of his star safety. “He’s not mindless, but he’s got that attitude that he’s ready to fight and mix it up. It doesn’t matter how big you are. He’s fearless.” That will always be a part of Branch’s game. He isn’t reckless, but he plays the game in a manner in which his opponents will always feel him. Most of the time, that is a positive. Especially in the hyper-competitive world that is the National Football League. However, other times it has bitten him, and that is where he is hoping to change. Controlled fury rather than completely losing your cool. You can read the entire story from Pompei right here , and learn how Branch’s love of his dog led him to make a life-changing friendship that put him on the course that he is currently on today. Plus, I don’t think anyone would complain about Philly getting pushed further down the standings. summary: The NFC isn’t looking quite as strong as it did, even a few weeks ago. This week kicked off with the Seattle Seahawks losing their third game of the season. full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell with quarterback Jared Goff (16) against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The NFC isn’t looking quite as strong as it did, even a few weeks ago. This week kicked off with the Seattle Seahawks losing their third game of the season. Last year, the defending Super Bowl champions lost only three games for the entire 2025 season. What was thought to be clearly the best division in football—the NFC West—now just has a single team with a winning record. The 49ers are 5-0, the Seahawks are 3-3, the Los Angeles Rams are 2-3, and the Arizona Cardinals are just 1-4. Beyond that division, the NFC East is looking like a mess. The New York Giants and their very unconvincing 3-1-1 record lead the division, while everyone else is below .500. Personally, I had a belief that the Philadelphia Eagles would pull themselves out of their 2-3 hole, but with the news that quarterback Jalen Hurts is now on injured reserve indefinitely with a blood clot issue, I’m not sure Tanner McKee and his two career starts are ready to turn things around. Elsewhere, it doesn’t look like the Saints are as good as the Lions made them look in Week 1, but the Atlanta Falcons are on the rise. And, of course, the NFC North is pretty strong from top to bottom. So today’s Question of the Day is: Where do the Lions rank in the NFC right now? My answer: Officially, the Lions are in the seventh spot in the NFC, when it comes to playoff standings. The 49ers, Vikings, Giants, and Panthers all lead their divisions. While the three Wild Card teams are the Packers, Bears, and Lions, in that order. As to how I feel the Lions rank, there are two teams that are easily ahead of the Lions: the undefeated 49ers and Vikings. Say what you will about the Vikings’ resume or their offensive struggles, that defense is raising hell right now, and it’s seriously impressive. I don’t think I need to make a case for San Francisco. Personally, I still think the Rams are better than the Lions, and it will show in their next five games when Los Angeles plays the Cardinals, Raiders, Chargers, Commanders, and Cardinals. Nothing is guaranteed in the NFL, but that feels like five straight wins. We also have to talk about the Carolina Panthers. They may have a worse record (2-2) than the Lions (3-2), but they beat them straight up—and in fairly decisively fashion. Objectively, you have to give them the edge. A couple of weeks ago, I ranked the Lions’ third in the NFC North behind the Vikings and Bears , and I don’t think my opinion of the division has changed despite Green Bay’s statement win over Chicago last week. So that puts the 49ers, Vikings, Bears, Rams, and Panthers all ahead of Detroit. I think the Seahawks, Packers, and Falcons are all right there on the same tier with the Lions, and that’s it. So I’d have the Lions anywhere from sixth to ninth in the NFC. For now, I’ll put them at seventh because I still believe Seattle will turn things around despite some serious struggles on offense and a step back on defense. title: Packers Week 6 Snap Counts: Who played against the Dallas Cowboys?
summary: There were a lot of moving parts on the Green Bay Packers’ roster this week, as the team placed three contributors on the injured reserve. Who stepped in their place against the Dallas Cowboys? Let’s take a position-by-position look at who was on the field for the Packers on offense and defense in the team’s […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images There were a lot of moving parts on the Green Bay Packers’ roster this week, as the team placed three contributors on the injured reserve. Who stepped in their place against the Dallas Cowboys? Let’s take a position-by-position look at who was on the field for the Packers on offense and defense in the team’s Week 6 win , explaining what has changed with the group. Quarterback Jordan Love: 73 snaps Tyrod Taylor: 0 Nothing has changed here. Running Back Pierre Strong Jr.: 41 MarShawn Lloyd: 30 Kaleb Johnson: 2 For the second straight week, running back Kaleb Johnson has basically been a non-factor in the offense, following his fumble against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 4. Johnson only had nine snaps, all in the second half in garbage time, against the Chicago Bears in Week 5, while MarShawn Lloyd played 27 and Pierre Strong Jr. played 25. Snaps were split between Strong and Lloyd again this week, with Johnson getting even fewer looks. Interestingly, head coach Matt LaFleur has recently said that if Pierre Strong Jr., who was dealing with a hamstring issue earlier in the year, was healthy in Week 1, then Strong would have played for the team — despite being a member of the practice squad. Don’t be surprised if the Packers end up dropping Strong to the practice squad when Josh Jacobs is activated on Monday , but then the team ends up activating Strong as a game-day elevation while Johnson — who is under a three-year cost-controlled rookie contract — is scratched as a developmental prospect. None of the Packers’ running backs have posted great production this season, which is part their fault and part the fault of the offensive line. Here’s what their unit has produced: Lloyd: 48 carries for 122 yards (2.5 YPC) Johnson: 28 carries for 104 yards (3.7 YPC) Strong: 16 carries for 35 yards (2.2 YPC) Chris Brooks: 15 carries for 70 yards (4.7 YPC) — currently on the injured reserve Receiver Christian Watson: 66 Matthew Golden: 63 Savion Williams: 40 Bo Melton: 18 J. Michael Sturdivant: 2 Coleman Owen: 0 With Jayden Reed, the team’s preferred starting slot receiver, and Skyy Moore, the team’s next man up at the slot position, now both on injured reserve, the Packers pivoted to mostly playing Savion Williams, himself called up from the injured reserve this week, to play in the slot in Week 6. Bo Melton, who played the position in-game when Moore dropped out last week, also got some looks — as well as a few opportunities as an outside receiver. J. Michael Strudivant and Coleman Owen, who was called up from the practice squad this week, look like special teams contributors who are really on “receivers” in case of emergency. For what it’s worth, Owen was the team’s primary punt returner (mixed results in his first showing, as he fair caught a football around the five-yard line but also had a decent return when given the opportunity), while Sturdivant jumped up to being the “off returner” (essentially a lead blocker) in the kick return game for Melton, who was pushed to the team’s main kick returner. The team had to backfill at both returner positions after Moore’s injury. Tight End Tucker Kraft: 56 Mark Redman: 23 Josh Whyle: 15 Jonnu Smith: 9 Josh Whyle getting more snaps than Jonnu Smith is a little surprising here, but Tucker Kraft has been the number one tight end on the team all year, and Mark Redman has been the season-long tight end two by a good margin. It’ll be interesting to see if this Whyle-Smith dynamic is a one-off. Smith has played 101 snaps to Whyle’s 36 on offense this year. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 73 Laken Tomlinson: 73 Sean Rhyan: 73 Travis Glover: 73 Anthony Belton: 73 Kevin Zeitler: 0 Jacob Monk: 0 John Williams: 0 Nothing surprising here, as the Packers rolled out their line of Jordan Morgan, Laken Tomlinson, Sean Rhyan, Travis Glover and Anthony Belton (left to right) for another full game tonight. The question here is how much longer the team will keep Kevin Zeitler on the bench, as neither Tomlinson or Glover played great against the Cowboys. Defensive Line Karl Brooks: 47 Devonte Wyatt: 46 Chris McClellan: 39 Anthony Campbell: 31 The Packers were very thin on the interior defensive line this week, as they typically play five players at the position. This game, they only had four options, as Jonathan Ford and Javon Hargrave joined Warren Brinson on the injured reserve this week, all while Jordon Riley is working his way off the physically unable to perform list. Frequently, the team was in 3-4 looks where Chris McClellan took over as the nose tackle (a role Ford previously played) and the only player at the position on the bench was Anthony Campbell, who had only played nine NFL snaps prior to this game. They lucked out that the Cowboys decided to play a lot of light formations on offense, keeping the 3-4 personnel from being ground out in the running game. They might not be so lucky next week against the Detroit Lions. They need another body at the position. Edge Defender Lukas Van Ness: 42 Barryn Sorrell: 40 Brenton Cox Jr.: 38 Dani Dennis-Sutton: 35 Arron Mosby: 0 When Arron Mosby was called up from the practice squad, he was obviously going to contribute on special teams. Last season, for example, Mosby played 221 special teams snaps over 12 games for the Packers (18.4 per game) compared to just 17 defensive snaps (1.4 per game). Lukas Van Ness played a little less on defense than usual, but Green Bay generally splits snaps between Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox Jr. and Dani Dennis-Sutton evenly. Here are the season-long numbers at the position, defensively: Lukas Van Ness: 274 snaps Barryn Sorrell: 204 snaps Dani Dennis-Sutton: 181 snaps Brenton Cox Jr.: 179 snaps Off-Ball Linebacker Zaire Franklin: 77 Isaiah McDuffie: 42 Ty’Ron Hopper: 33 Nick Niemann: 0 Kristian Welch: 0 Since Edgerrin Cooper’s injury, Ty’Ron Hopper has played 72 snaps of defense to Isaiah McDuffie’s 74. They tend to draft off drives about every two drives, likely to try to keep their legs fresh for special teams. For perspective, McDuffie ranked second on the team in special teams reps going into this week, while Hopper ranked fifth. Nick Niemann (first in special teams) and Kristian Welch are on pretty incredible special teams pace, too, which is why they’re on the game-day roster. Welch has only been on the roster for three weeks, but is basically matching Niemann’s pace when he’s up from the practice squad. Cornerback Keisean Nixon: 77 Brandon Cisse: 54 Carrington Valentine: 25 Kamal Hadden: 0 The Packers played two snaps of dime defense this week in third-and-long looks, which pushes Carrington Valentine into the slot. They seem to be treating their second slot in dime looks differently than true slot defenders, as Kamal Hadden (who got in at the position late in the Bears game in garbage time) is actually the “next man up” at the position. Brandon Cisse, the team’s right cornerback, suffered a stinger, which pushed Valentine up to outside cornerback in this game, too. Cisse never returned to action, but he stated after the game to Packers.com’s Weston Hodkiewicz that he’s “ fine .” Cisse was the only player in Week 6 who dropped out and did not return to play. Progress! Also: Both Keisean Nixon and Cisse had pretty good games. Cisse was probably having his best game as a Packer before his injury. Valentine almost got two interceptions in his limited playing time, too. Safety Xavier McKinney: 77 Evan Williams: 77 Javon Bullard: 66 Kitan Oladapo: 0 The only notable thing here is that slot defender Javon Bullard played six-sevenths of snaps on defense, meaning that the Packers played a lot of nickel personnel in this game. As we mentioned in the defensive line section, Green Bay wasn’t forced to play their 3-4 base defense often (usually, it’s around one-third of their snaps, but varies a good amount from team to team), which really bailed out their thin line. Like the deep linebackers, Kitan Oladapo…

title: Packers-Cowboys Final Score: Green Bay defense dominates Dallas on ‘Sunday Night Football’
summary: The Dallas Cowboys came into Lambeau Field on Sunday Night Football with a high-powered offense. Dak Prescott and company led the offense in many drive-based statistics, including the percentage of offensive drives ending in a score, plays per drive, and yards per drive. Against Jonathan Gannon’s aggressive Green Bay Packers defense, the Cowboys managed just […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 18: Evan Williams #33 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates an interception during the second quarter against the Dallas Cowboys at Lambeau Field on October 18, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys came into Lambeau Field on Sunday Night Football with a high-powered offense. Dak Prescott and company led the offense in many drive-based statistics, including the percentage of offensive drives ending in a score, plays per drive, and yards per drive. Against Jonathan Gannon’s aggressive Green Bay Packers defense, the Cowboys managed just seven points on nine offensive drives as the green and gold expanded their league-leading interception numbers. Evan Williams and rookie Brandon Cisse each picked off Dak Prescott, who was under pressure all night long, as the defense led the way in a 23-13 win that improved the Packers’ record to 4-2. Prescott’s counterpart, Jordan Love, shook off an early interception of his own to put up a high-quality performance. That pick could have been a truly game-changing play, as it was originally returned for a touchdown that would have tied the game at 7 early on. Instead, the scoring return was nullified on review and the Packers’ defense ended up getting a stop to keep Dallas off the scoreboard. The Packers’ offense went on to convert each of their first seven third-down opportunities and finished 11-of-18 for the game as Love delivered under pressure time and time again. Ultimately, Love failed to record multiple touchdown passes for the first time in a game all season, but it wasn’t for lack of trying; he saw three potential touchdown passes get dropped by his receivers, but still managed to throw for 276 yards. Matthew Golden was the biggest offender, with two of those dropped scores and a third drop later in the game, but he did end the game with an excellent stat line: six catches for 104 yards and the only receiving touchdown of the game. Additionally, Love did end up being responsible for a second touchdown, getting the Packers’ other score on a quarterback sneak just before halftime as the team led 17-0 heading into the break. The Green Bay defense kept up its excellent play in the second half. After giving up a single touchdown early in the third quarter, they forced turnovers on downs twice in the fourth before allowing a touchdown in garbage time while holding a 16-point lead — though they came up with a big stop on the two-point conversion to largely put an end to the game. A year after combining for 80 points in a 40-40 tie, Green Bay’s new-look defense was the story. For the first time since 2016, the Packers now have a three-game streak of holding opponents to 14 points or fewer. And they have done this without Micah Parsons available yet this season. The Packers deferred after winning the opening kickoff and the decision paid off; the defense forced a punt on Dallas’ opening possession, allowing one first down before getting off the field. With the offense starting at the 10-yard line, Jordan Love amassed 109 passing yards on the Packers’ first series, thanks to a combination of penalties and lost yardage on run plays. The drive ended in the end zone as Love found Matthew Golden for a 9-yard touchdown, giving the Packers an early lead. AGENT 0 📺: NBC pic.twitter.com/g9gZwas6JN — Green Bay Packers (@packers) October 19, 2026 Green Bay’s defense forced a 3-and-out on the next Cowboys possession, aided by a pair of first-down penalties, and practice squad call-up Coleman Owen picked up 16 yards on a punt return to set up the Packers at the 41-yard line. However, on second down, linebacker Dee Winters jumped Love’s pass for Golden and picked it off, returning the interception all the way into the end zone. Upon review, the officials determined that Golden touched Winters down as he made the catch, taking away the points and leaving Dallas with the ball at the Packers’ 42-yard line. Once those points came off the board, the Cowboys failed to put them back on. Prescott connected with CeeDee Lamb for a 16-yard gain on the Cowboys first third down attempt of the drive, reaching the Packers’ red zone for the first time, but his next two passes hit yellow gloves. He took a big hit from Zaire Franklin and lofted a pass to the end zone that was nearly intercepted by Brandon Cisse, then didn’t see Evan Williams dropping in coverage as the Packers’ safety stepped in front of a pass and returned the turnover favor with an interception of his own, his second in three games. Love got the offense moving, first with a check-down to Pierre Strong for a third-down conversion and then a 28-yard gain to Christian Watson over the middle. The Packers later ran a read-option at Rashan Gary, who bit hard on the running back and allowed Love to run for 13 and a first down. Green Bay couldn’t punch the ball into the end zone on a few opportunities near the goal line, eventually settling for a short field goal to extend their lead to 10-0. Matthew Golden dropped a walk-in touchdown earlier on the drive, however, seemingly losing the ball in the Lambeau Field lights and costing the Packers four points as a result. Dallas got its first long drive of the game going on the next series, reaching Packers territory just before the two-minute warning, but on their first play out of the timeout, Brandon Cisse got his first interception as a pro. CeeDee Lamb slipped on the Lambeau Field turf and Prescott’s throw went straight to Cisse. The Packers’ offense looked like it would go without a score late, but they got the benefit of a huge pass interference penalty on Joey Porter, Jr., who pushed Bo Melton out of bounds with the ball in the air. That 37-yard flag set up the Packers well inside field goal range. After dropping another potential touchdown, Golden hauled in a brilliant catch on 3rd down, setting up goal-to-go with a 21-yard gain at just under 30 seconds to go. After another DPI in the end zone, Love took a quarterback sneak into the end zone behind right guard Travis Glover, expanding the lead to 17-0 just before halftime. Sean Rhyan committed a holding penalty on the first play of the second half, setting the Packers back behind the sticks and leading to a three-and-out. Jonathan Mingo returned Daniel Whelan’s first punt of the game to just across midfield, where Dallas got their offense underway for the second half. After Prescott scrambled for a few yards on 3rd-and-long, Lamb picked up 18 yards over the middle on 4th-and-2 with Cisse trailing. A few plays later, Javonte Williams pushed into the end zone from a yard out, getting the Cowboys on the board. Green Bay avoided a negative play on first down on the next drive, getting a short run from Strong, then got another first down on third-and-short from Love to Watson. The team faced a 4th-and-3 from Dallas’ 44 a few plays later, but Love found Kraft up the left sideline for a run-and-catch of 14 yards. That got the Packers into Trey Smack’s range, and after yet another drop in the end zone — Watson couldn’t come up with a touchdown off the slightest of deflections by a Cowboys defender — he drilled a 44-yard field goal to make the score 20-7. Jonathan Gannon dialed up pressure on Prescott on the next drive, forcing a punt as Evan Williams came unblocked and led to an incomplete pass on third down. Former Packer Kenny Clark sacked Love on third down on the next series, however, bringing on Daniel Whelan to punt out of his own end zone. He got a good one off and the Cowboys were flagged for holding on the kick, setting them up back at their own 30. The Packers seemed poised to get a quick three-and-out, but rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton was flagged for taunting, offsetting a penalty on Dallas, and the C0wboys converted their second try on 3rd-and-6. Gannon brought pressure again on 3rd-and-2 a few plays later, bringing up yet another 4th down, this time from midfield. This time, Javon Bullard…

full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers announced on Sunday that, along with cornerback Benjamin St-Juste, who was already ruled out with an injury, the team has ruled out three offensive linemen against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 6: Jager Burton, Aaron Banks and Donovan Jennings. At times, both Glover and Williams, who are both active today, had been healthy scratches while Jennings was playing with the first-team offense. Clearly, the coaching staff has decided their early-season plan at the position wasn’t the best route to follow any longer. The scratch announcements also mean that receiver Savion Williams (questionable), defensive lineman Anthony Campbell (questionable) and cornerback Brandon Cisse (questionable) will be up for game day. title: Packers-Cowboys preview: How Dallas schemes up shot plays
summary: So far through Week 5, the Dallas Cowboys and quarterback Dak Prescott have thrown 18 passes 20+ yards downfield. That may not seem like a lot, but Prescott has connected on eight of those passes for two touchdowns and 271 yards, ranking 9th in yardage. And he has a variety of weapons around him that […]
full_text: (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images So far through Week 5, the Dallas Cowboys and quarterback Dak Prescott have thrown 18 passes 20+ yards downfield. That may not seem like a lot, but Prescott has connected on eight of those passes for two touchdowns and 271 yards, ranking 9th in yardage. And he has a variety of weapons around him that give him the confidence to push the ball deep. The Cowboys’ primary non-play-action shot play is “989.” 989 is a three verticals passing concept. Both outside receivers run go routes, the inside receiver runs a post or middle read, and the quarterback throws to whichever deep matchup the safeties fail to cover. It is one of the oldest dropback shots in football and still a weekly call for offenses built around an elite outside receiver. What is 989 The name is the play call, and legendary San Diego Chargers head coach Don Coryell made it a staple. His playbook featured dozens and dozens of plays represented by a number system. Each receiver gets one digit, assigned in a fixed order starting with the X on the single-receiver side, and each digit is a branch of the route tree. The above image is from Marty Schottenheimer’s 2005 Chargers playbook, the father of current Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer. In that tree, even numbers break inside, odd numbers break outside, and the 9 is the straight vertical exception. An 8 is the post. So 989 reads X go, Y post, Z go. Teams outside the Coryell tree usually call the same idea “double go” or “double go, middle read.” The concept is deliberately simple. It isolates the two outside receivers one-on-one against corners and uses the inside vertical to occupy the deep middle. Its value is less in clever structure than in what it forces a defense to show about its safeties before the ball comes out. Only three players run routes that matter. Everyone else exists to buy time for a throw that travels 40-plus yards. The X receiver, aligned to the single-receiver side, runs the 9. He wins vertically with whatever release he judges best and protects the space between the numbers and the sideline. The Z receiver on the field side runs the same 9 with the same rule. The quarterback may pre-select this side if it offers the better matchup. The Y or slot receiver runs the 8, which in modern versions is a middle read. Against two-high safeties, with the middle of the field open, he runs the post. Against a single-high safety, with the middle of the field closed, he converts to a 10-to-12-yard in route (a “basic”) or a dig. The back and any extra tight end stay in to protect or chip the edges, then release late as the checkdown. How it attacks coverage It can attack each coverage in a variety of ways. One deep safety cannot help on both sidelines, and two deep safeties leave a seam between them. Whatever shell the defense shows, one of the three routes is aimed at the hole it creates. Cover 1 (man-free). Both outside receivers are one-on-one, and the free safety can help on only one side. The ball goes to the go route the safety does not favor, after the quarterback moves him with his eyes. Cover 3. Each outside-third corner carries a vertical alone, and a post would run straight into the free safety. The quarterback looks to the outside go against the weaker corner while the inside route flattens under the safety. Cover 2. The safeties help over the top outside, which leaves the deep middle and the sideline window behind the corner soft. The post splits the safeties first, then the quarterback looks to the “hole shot” between the corner and safety. Tampa 2. The middle linebacker carries the deep middle, so the inside route stops short in front of him instead of finishing the post. That route instead converts to more of a dig route over the middle and the quarterback can then take a hole shot between the corner and safety. Quarters. The safeties key the inside receiver’s vertical, and a more vertical post stresses that rule. The post is there if the safety bites or squats. If he stays on top, the ball goes to the go route on the isolated side. 2-Man. The defenders underneath trail their receivers while the safeties cap the outside. The post splits the safeties over a trailing defender. The quarterback’s read The read starts before the snap. The quarterback identifies the shell, picks the outside matchup he likes, and then reads that matchup against the middle route. Checkdowns come last. Against a closed middle (one-high), his first look is the preferred outside go, the matchup he picked pre-snap. Second is the middle route, now flattened under the safety. That is often a tight window, since the safety and hook defenders bracket it. Third is the back or tight end releasing late after protecting. Against an open middle (two-high), the progression flips. The middle read splitting the safeties comes first, the hole shot down the sideline behind the corner comes second, and the late-releasing back or tight end comes third. The safety is the quarterback’s real assignment. Against Detroit’s Cover 1 robber in 2021, Rodgers held the middle safety with his eyes long enough for Davante Adams to win on an out-and-up down the left side. Tom Brady did the same in Tampa, using his eyes to hold or shift the free safety before throwing outside. The Cowboys and 989 It has been a staple passing concept for the Cowboys this season with Prescott hitting both the outside vertical and the inside seam routes. In overtime of their 2025 game against the Packers, a game they tied 40-40, the Cowboys moved the ball with ease on the defense, hitting two explosive pass plays. The second pass they hit was a bit of luck, catching the Packers’ defense gasping for air. But on the first pass they hit, they took advantage of a common defensive call on third down. The defense is showing cover-3 or a possible blitz/pressure with man coverage. The post-snap reveals cover-2 invert, which we have covered here extensively since Hafley took over. The Cowboys are running “989” here. The defense presented the same alignment before spinning the coverage to cover-2 invert. Prescott saw the pre-snap alignment again and audibled the play to a more favorable concept to beat the coverage, betting that in a similar down and distance, the Packers would rotate again to 2-invert. He guessed right. As the corner bailed diagonally to the deep half in between the numbers and hash and away from the sideline, Pickens got open on the vertical to the single receiver side and Prescott dropped it in before the coverage could get to it. On the crucial play in overtime, the Cowboys called the same “989” concept again. This time, the Packers defense had the outside routes covered up playing cover-3 while the inside post route was wide open. Pressure forced Prescott to escape the pocket; otherwise, he likely would have hit the throw over the middle for a big gain. Keisean Nixon was the outside corner covering Jalen Tolbert. When Prescott escaped, the offense went into scramble drill mode. Tolbert slipped, and Nixon let up. But Tolbert quickly got up and presented himself as a target, working back down to the throw 34 yards away. Prescott launched it rolling to his right, and Tolbert came up with the toe-drag catch on the sideline while Nixon could only watch helplessly. Final thoughts 989 is a talent-forcing play. It hands the defense a simple question: How many safeties will you commit deep? Every answer costs something. Against one-high, the offense gets its best receiver isolated outside. Against two-high, it gets a post between the safeties. The concept fails mainly when the line cannot hold up or when the outside receivers cannot beat their man. That is why it is a good diagnostic for film study. When a team calls 989, watch three things: the shell at the snap, where the quarterback’s eyes put the safety, and how many bodies stay in to protect. Those three details usually explain the result better than the throw itself. The…

Houston, now at 2-4 but having won two straight road games against division rivals, returns to NRG Stadium to host the New York Giants of New Jersey. The Giants, sitting at 3-2-1, come into this matchup atop the NFC East, despite not winning in their last two games, a tie at Washington and a loss against New Orleans. In their last game, they fell to the Saints 34-27, but the Saints held a lead of 34-10 at one point in the 4th Quarter. The Giants, forced to start backup QB Jameis Winston since starter Jaxson Dart went down with a season-ending injury, decided to give recent trade acquisition J.J. McCarthy a chance in the 4th quarter. McCarthy went 11-of-21 for 243 yards for 1 TD and 1 INT, and had the Giants in position to possibly tie or win on the final Giants’ drive of the game. The New York/New Jersey sports pages will have themselves a field day talking about the QB spot in this coming week. Likely because of that QB uncertainty, along with Houston’s recent winning streak and the supposed talent disparity, the opening odds from FanDuel for the upcoming matchup between the Texans and the Giants are strongly supporting Houston at home: Overall, this may seem a bit high of an opening line. However, the Texans, even coming off a huge win against Jacksonville, are still struggling on defense and sit at 0-3 at home. They have only beaten the Giants once in 6 total meetings, and that was in 2002. Sandwiched between an international game and a bye week, this has the feel of a trap game for Houston. title: RECAP: Texans Win by Last-Second Field Goal over Jaguars, 34-31
summary: Finally, the Texans get a big time stop and win a close game! The last time the Texans played in London at Wembley Stadium, they defeated the Jacksonville Jaguars 26-3 in November to improve to 6-3 on the 2019 season. This year, the Texans would kill to have a record like that and be in […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 18: Ka'imi Fairbairn of the Houston Texans kicks a field goal in the fourth quarter during the NFL London Series match between Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium on October 18, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Julian Finney/Getty Images) | Getty Images Finally, the Texans get a big time stop and win a close game! The last time the Texans played in London at Wembley Stadium, they defeated the Jacksonville Jaguars 26-3 in November to improve to 6-3 on the 2019 season. This year, the Texans would kill to have a record like that and be in such a position, but, even though this game was much, much closer and featured a 1-4 Texans squad clinging to their playoff hopes against a great 4-1 Jaguars team, the Texans chances of making a comeback this season were not completely gone just yet, and a big win here in London could be the impetus to a late-season surge, not dissimilar from what they experience in 2025. If they could just win this game, a lot of the missteps from September could be forgotten. Well, knowing the Texans, they weren’t going to make it easy, and this one would go back and forth and feature mistakes by the Texans on defense all over the field, multiple missed tackles, and poor coverage on special teams. But, when it came down to the end of the game, the Texans did something they had failed to do all season yet: they tightened up on defense, held the opponent to a field goal, and put the game away with a game-winning drive on offense! There were still a lot of mistakes by the Texans in this game, but if there’s a few things they can leave this game with that they can be proud of, it’s that they finally found a way to win, AND have a MVP-caliber quarterback in CJ Stroud: WHAT A CATCH FROM NICO COLLINS HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FSlix6VI5c — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Texans QB CJ Stroud opened the game up on the same hot streak he’s been on all season, and it continued for…nearly the entire game! He got huge completions out of WR Nico Collins and a touchdown grab from TE Foster Moreau to end the first quarter, but the Jaguars offense – led by QB Trevor Lawrence, RB Bhayshul Tuten, and WRs Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers – were able to march up and down the chewed up Wembley Stadium pitch all game long. On their third drive, the Jaguars were able to pound the ball into the red zone, but Lawrence would throw an interception in the end zone to Calen Bullock! Calen Bullock picks it off in the end zone for the @HoustonTexans ! HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/3EBfQmbmWr — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 You may have hoped that this interception have been a sign that the defense was finally turning the page on what has been a rough start to the season, but…nope! Just like the Buffalo Bills and Dallas Cowboys games, the Texans defense rarely pressured the quarterback and repeatedly missed tackles on the Jags’ tailbacks Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. and CB/WR Travis Hunter. Fortunately, Stroud would continue to play well the entire first half, finding TE Dalton Schultz, WR Jaylin Noel, and recent trade acquisition WR Marvin Harrison Jr. for big completions. The game went back and forth in the second quarter, with Jacksonville taking a 17-14 lead following a two-yard touchdown reception by Tuten: Nice design by Coen. Good play by Tuten. Terrible by Blakenship. Azeez got hurt here. Hard to speculate what happened. Move Henry To’oTo’o to MLB & Hansen to WLB. pic.twitter.com/UPFwjfYqls — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) October 18, 2026 Bhayshul Tuten gets his second TD of the day! HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rjs9PpK7cn — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Stroud would NOT be one-upped by Lawrence before the half was over, though. On Houston’s following drive, they would go 63 yards on three plays, highlighted by amazing, 50-yard pass to Jaylin Noel and then one of the best touchdown receptions you’ll ever see from Foster Moreau for Houston to regain the lead at halftime: WHAT A THROW FROM CJ STROUD. HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Z8LUxZceAl — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 An absolutely perfect throw from CJ Stroud for the touchdown HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Ebmjyao7cO — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Following halftime, the Texans would receive the ball and obtain the ever-elusive “double dip,” or, scoring a touchdown at the end of the first half and then scoring again right at the beginning of the second half. Stroud would get more action out of Noel and Harrison on this drive, but also be complemented by the first adequate rushes by RBs Woody Marks and Jawhar Jordan, who was filling in for an injured RB David Montgomery. Now, with a 24-14 lead following an impressive touchdown reception to Noel, the Texans looked in control of the game, even if their defense still couldn’t stop a nosebleed. Another MHJ catch for a first down HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/YVd7AMSzTR — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Another dime from CJ Stroud, touchdown @HoustonTexans ! HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/volhpIM4kI — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 After this drive, the Texans defense actually forces their second (and last) punt of the game against the Jaguars, but the Texans offense can’t capitalize, and sends the ball back Jacksonville’s way after a disappointing five-play drive that ended in a Kai Kroeger punt. Jacksonville’s responded to the gift Houston had bestowed upon them with another touchdown drive. Jags’ WR Jakobi Meyers tore up Texans LB Hentry To’oTo’o and Calen Bullock, and then Jags’ rookie TE Nate Boerkircher challenges Foster Moreau’s fantastic touchdown catch with an impressive one of his one against Texans S M.J. Stewart, making the game 24-21 Texans: Nate Boerkircher with the INSANE one-handed touchdown catch! HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/oBhAyPowx9 — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 The highlights just don’t stop coming in this game! Now, you start to get the feeling that neither team’s defense is going to be able to stop all of these highlights from the quarterbacks and pass catchers, and the game seems like it’s going to be determined by who has the ball last. So, of course, Houston follows Jacksonville’s touchdown drive with another quick, five-play touchdown drive of their own, highlighted by a defensive pass interference penalty on Jags’ CB Jarrian Jones trying to cover WR Nico Collins, followed by a brilliant cut-back run by RB Jawhar Jordan: The cutback and vision from Jawhar Jordan on this touchdown run 🔥 HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/xRtD213b8j — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 This game is really starting to go crazy now, and the Texans are just looking for somewhere to land the plane! Can’t do it yet, cuz now the Jaguars are unleashing CB/WR Travis Hunter on the offensive side of the ball, and he makes LBs To’oTo’o and Azeez Al-Shaair (who briefly left the game to enter the concussion protocol, then returned in the third quarter) look silly on this reception and following touchdown grab: Travis Hunter breaking tackles left and right out there HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/PpIhEZZvYv — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 TRAVIS HUNTER TOUCHDOWN! HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/UEbQwJYHqy — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Now, it’s 31-28 Houston, and you get the feeling the Texans need to ice this game by getting a touchdown on this upcoming drive with 11:26 remaining in the fourth quarter, lest they leave the door open for Jacksonville to snatch the game away. And, for the first time this season, the Texans are actually able to run the ball well? Woody Marks and Jawhar Jordan march the Texans downfield, with Marks becoming the first RB to eclipse the 40-yard rushing mark against this Jaguars defense, but…

title: This is the beginning of the end for this iteration of the Colts
summary: The Chris Ballard era is over. Shane Steichen at the helm is no more. Daniel Jones as the quarterback for the Indianapolis Colts is on incredibly thin ice. Losing to the Tennessee Titans sure feels like the straw that will break the camel’s back. For a season in which the motto is “Find a Way”, […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 18: Head coach Shane Steichen of the Indianapolis Colts looks on during the fourth quarter against the Tennessee Titans at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chris Ballard era is over. Shane Steichen at the helm is no more. Daniel Jones as the quarterback for the Indianapolis Colts is on incredibly thin ice. Losing to the Tennessee Titans sure feels like the straw that will break the camel’s back. For a season in which the motto is “Find a Way”, the only thing this organization needs to find a way to do is to push the reset button. It’s been six weeks, so saying it’s all over is tough. A lot can change with two-thirds of the season left. The biggest issue is the here and now. After falling to the winless Titans at home, the Colts find themselves at 2-4. That is the now. The immediate future is bleak as well. Not to say that the Colts can’t win but the undefeated Vikings and the Jaguars, both on the road, lie ahead. Ask yourself if you see those games going well. Time is up. The beginning part of this season was do or die. Finding a way didn’t mean find a way to lose to the worst team in football. Props to the Colts for finding creative ways to lose, but that isn’t what Carlie Irsay-Gordon had in mind. Ballard’s seat is so hot that it should have already melted. Steichen hasn’t shown enough to make it out of this. The failures are evident and felt by the players too. This is rock bottom and change is needed. Patience is a virtue, but it isn’t a requirement in the NFL. The Irsays have shown enough over the years to this staff and personnel. Daniel Jones doesn’t have the juice. Shane Steichen has shown an inability to win. Chris Ballard has failed to put a good product on the field 90% of the time. We knew this was coming. Sunday’s disaster was the gust of wind that will topple this house of cards.
