title: Colts franchise falls to new low of mediocrity after being upset at home by once winless Titans
summary: In what was nothing short of a gut punch to their season and ever-dwindling playoff hopes, the Indianapolis Colts (2-4) were upset by the once winless Tennessee Titans (1-5), 26-20, at home on Sunday afternoon. It was a game that the Colts simply couldn’t afford to lose, as there won’t be an easier game on […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 18: Jermaine Johnson II #11 of the Tennessee Titans celebrates after sacking Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts during the second quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images In what was nothing short of a gut punch to their season and ever-dwindling playoff hopes, the Indianapolis Colts (2-4) were upset by the once winless Tennessee Titans (1-5), 26-20, at home on Sunday afternoon. It was a game that the Colts simply couldn’t afford to lose, as there won’t be an easier game on their schedule this entire remaining 2o26 regular season. The AFC South division Jacksonville Jaguars even narrowly fell to the Houston Texans in London, but the Colts couldn’t even make up divisional standings ground by losing to the lowly Titans of all teams. Specifically, the Colts were at home, hosting a winless Titans team that hadn’t won since December 21st of last year, had an 11-game AFC South losing streak, and held a rather convincing 13-0 lead at halftime in this one. It’s not that the Colts were dominating the Titans by any stretch, but it felt like Indianapolis had firm control of the game’s outcome at intermission and short of beating themselves frequently, would rather handedly outlast Tennessee to the game’s final whistle—probably to the tune of double digits. However, beat themselves, Indianapolis did and did too often , with a fumble lost, an interception, and a blocked punt returned for a touchdown—all in the second half. It’s not that the Titans played great or caught fire after halftime, the Colts just beat themselves with turnovers compiled with poor football collectively, I mean 0 defensive sacks and 1 QB hit on the afternoon to the Titans 6 sacks and 11 QB hits? In a game where Colts legends were in the house to honor Hall of Fame placekicker Adam Vinatieri’s halftime induction into the franchise’s ring of honor, including, Dallas Clark, Dwight Freeney, Tarik Glenn, Edgerrin James, Robert Mathis, and Bill Polian, there was nothing legendary about this Colts second half performance. It was closer to putrid or resembling the Covenant grunts I used to lay waste to in “legendary mode” in Halo 2 during my high school years as the Master Chief. In 2024 after starting quarterback Anthony Richardson was infamously benched following an in-game “tap-out,” former retired Pro Bowl center Ryan Kelly alluded to a high standard that each member of the team, including the young Richardson, needed to hold themselves to, but at this point, what is that standard anymore? Does anyone actually know it, remember it, or embody it? It seems to be descending lower and lower by the week. As one of the few remaining longtime leaders who’s consistently represented the franchise’s once proud standard, Pro Bowl veteran defensive tackle DeForest Buckner frustratingly stated post-game, “Yeah, I’m pissed off too. I’m sick and tired of the same song and dance every year.” For a Colts franchise that’s finished 8-9 for two straight seasons and no better than 8-9 (once) over the past five seasons, having not made the playoffs since 2020 during the COVID-19 year, this felt like a new low of mediocrity regarding the Horseshoe—and fans are rightfully frustrated, even chanting ‘Fire Ballard’ for those that remained with the contest already decided at the disappointing game’s final conclusion.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Your resident Colts optimist has nothing for you.
summary: Throughout an uneven (at best) start to the season, I’ve been able to see a way forward to the Colts playing well and having a good season. If it went well enough to save some jobs and brighten the outlook among fans, that would be great, but mostly it is because I honestly felt that […]
full_text: Throughout an uneven (at best) start to the season, I’ve been able to see a way forward to the Colts playing well and having a good season. If it went well enough to save some jobs and brighten the outlook among fans, that would be great, but mostly it is because I honestly felt that the pieces were in place for success. I’ve tried to wish and squint the stink off of this team, but whatever settles to the bottom when cream rises to the top, is what we are, six games through the season. I’ve argued or at least offered a different opinion for those wanting to “burn it down”, for long enough. Fire everyone? Fine. Trade away assets for future considerations? Why not? Hand AR the keys? Not sure what he would be driving, but sure, go for it. Absolutely nothing would surprise me as far as a press conference would look in the aftermath of today’s game. Seriously, how could it get worse? I’m not seeing anything that would suggest that this team, as assembled, can compete with the rest of the NFL. They might win a game here and there, because “Any given Sunday”, but I would find it hard to believe that we would be favored in any game left on the schedule, sans Miami. If Steichen is allowed another press conference, I don’t want to watch. “We/I need to be better” should cause each reporter to just turn off the recording devices and walk out. I’d like to think that the team wanted to win, at least as much as I do, but I don’t see much evidence of it. I honestly think that the talent level among all 32 teams in not separated by that much (aside from QB) and the difference in results depends on coaching, effort, and luck. We are big fat 0 – 3 in those three. I’ll cool off and write something more constructive after the butt hurt has subsided, but this is my effort after watching the effort I witnessed today.

title: It’s time to blow it up: The Colts need to fire Chris Ballard and Shane Steichen
summary: Enough. The Tennessee Titans walked into Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday at 0-5. They had scored three points the previous week, entered the afternoon averaging 11.6 points per game and looked every bit like one of the worst teams in football. The Colts led them 13-0 at halftime and somehow lost 26-20. Tennessee picked up […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - JULY 27: Indianapolis Colts general manager Chris Ballard and Indianapolis Colts head coach Shane Steichen talk on the field during the Indianapolis Colts training camp practice on July 27, 2024 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Enough. The Tennessee Titans walked into Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday at 0-5. They had scored three points the previous week, entered the afternoon averaging 11.6 points per game and looked every bit like one of the worst teams in football. The Colts led them 13-0 at halftime and somehow lost 26-20. Tennessee picked up its first victory of the season, Indianapolis fell to 2-4 and a game that should have been one of the easiest remaining wins on the schedule instead became one of the most embarrassing losses of the Chris Ballard era. The Titans even scored a late touchdown off a blocked punt because apparently struggling on offense and defense was not enough; special teams needed to join the party too. I have written about firing Ballard before. I have written about firing Lou Anarumo. I have criticized Shane Steichen plenty over the last few seasons. At this point, separating all of these problems almost feels pointless because the entire operation looks broken. Fire Ballard. Fire Steichen. If Anarumo goes with them, fine by me. Put interim people in charge, let them get through January and start preparing for an offseason where this organization finally gets a new direction. This is not a playoff team right now, and it does not look particularly close to being one. Sunday should be the game that finally ends the argument. This is the roster Chris Ballard built Ballard is in his 10th season as general manager of the Indianapolis Colts. Before this season, his teams were 70-78-1 with two playoff appearances, one playoff victory and zero AFC South championships. Add this year and the record is now 72-82-1. Ten years, zero division titles. That is not a temporary slump, a rebuild that needs another offseason or the product of one unfortunate quarterback injury. It’s the résumé. It’s who he is! This is what the Colts have been under Chris Ballard. Sunday was almost a condensed version of every roster-building issue that has followed him around. The Colts were missing Alec Pierce, Tyler Warren and Ashton Dulin, which left Daniel Jones throwing primarily to Josh Downs, 31-year-old Laquon Treadwell and 34-year-old Keenan Allen, with Will Mallory taking on a bigger role at tight end. Injuries are obviously part of that, but the problem is what happens when those injuries arrive. Good rosters lose starters and still have functional NFL players waiting behind them. Bad rosters suddenly look like this one. Pierce is the perfect example. His heel was already a known concern after offseason surgery, yet Indianapolis entered the year without much proven insurance behind him. Once Pierce aggravated the injury, the Colts reacted by signing Darius Slayton in late September. He never played a snap, struggled to get integrated, dealt with a knee injury and was released less than a month later. That is not preparation. That is scrambling after the emergency has already arrived. The same problem exists at offensive tackle. Braden Smith is gone, and instead of adding a legitimate veteran option, Ballard decided the Colts had enough internally. Jalen Travis has been one of the players asked to fill that void, and Sunday was another example of how badly that bet has gone. The tackles were overwhelmed, with Travis in particular looking completely overmatched. Jones deserves plenty of criticism for his performance, but playing quarterback becomes much more difficult when the edges of the pocket collapse and your depleted receiving corps is not consistently separating. Ballard has always preached development. Draft your guys, trust your guys and give them opportunities. There is nothing wrong with that philosophy when the players are good enough. Sometimes, however, “your guys” simply are not good enough, and after ten years that excuse has worn extremely thin. Daniel Jones is not the answer, and Steichen has not helped him Jones was terrible Sunday. His decision-making was poor, his arm looked weak and his game deteriorated quickly whenever Tennessee generated pressure. There were throws where he looked uncomfortable before the play ever had a chance to develop, and there simply are not enough high-end physical traits left to compensate when everything around him starts breaking down. This has not come completely out of nowhere either. Entering Sunday, Jones had only three touchdown passes against four interceptions in five games while averaging 5.8 yards per attempt with a 73.6 passer rating. He showed enough against Kansas City to remind everyone there is still some talent there, and the finish against Houston was encouraging, but the overall trend has been ugly. Steichen attached his offense to Jones after the success they had early last season, and I understood the logic. Before the Achilles injury, Jones played legitimately good football in 2025 and Steichen got more out of him than the Giants consistently did. That pairing gave the Colts a reason to believe it could work again. It clearly is not working right now. What bothers me more is how little the offense seems to be doing to compensate. If your quarterback struggles against pressure, your tackles cannot protect him and half of your receiving corps is injured, the structure of the offense needs to change. Find easier completions. Move the pocket. Use more misdirection. Manufacture touches. Get Jonathan Taylor more involved in the passing game. Give Jones throws where he does not have to stand in a collapsing pocket, process everything perfectly and then make a difficult throw to a receiver struggling to separate. Instead, the offense too often looks like it is asking mediocre players to simply play better. Anthony Richardson is sitting there, and if Indianapolis wants to give him another look, go ahead. Just do not pretend changing quarterbacks suddenly fixes the team. Richardson is not walking onto the field and magically rescuing this offense, and Riley Leonard is not either. The entire quarterback room has questions, the tackles are struggling, the receiver group is depleted and Taylor cannot carry the offense by himself every Sunday. Put whoever you want behind center. The problems are much bigger than one player. That brings Steichen into the conversation because this is his side of the football. The 2025 offense was legitimately good before the season collapsed, finishing eighth in points per game, ninth in yards and second in points per drive. There was a time when his offensive coaching was the best argument for keeping him. Six games into 2026, I have no idea what this offense is supposed to be. The turnovers have been brutal, the passing game lacks explosiveness, Taylor has spent too much time fighting for yards behind an inconsistent line and Jones looks significantly worse. The depth is bad, but the coaching staff has not found enough ways to hide it. Steichen is now 27-30 as Colts head coach and has never made the playoffs. Indianapolis went 9-8 in his first year, followed that with consecutive 8-9 seasons and is now 2-4. As the kids say, that’s mid. The more concerning trend is what has happened in close games. Indianapolis went 14-8 in one-score games over Steichen’s first two seasons, then went 3-7 last year and is 1-2 this season. That makes the Colts 4-9 in one-score games since the beginning of 2025, despite spending the offseason talking about how badly they needed to finish games better. There is another ugly part of Steichen’s record. Entering Sunday, the Colts were 7-25 against teams with winning records under him. At least they had generally handled bad opponents, going 19-5 against teams below .500. That was the floor. They might not beat…

title: Indianapolis Colts discussion: Week 6 live chat during the Titans game
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are at home to take on the Tennessee Titans for week 6 of the 2026 season, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. Last week we saw the Colts march into Pittsburgh and helped Aaron Rodgers turn back the clock, made sure he looked much younger than his 42 years would suggest. The game wasn’t […]
full_text: Stella Steichen plays with the Indianapolis Colts mascot, Blue, while her father, Shane Steichen speaks at a press conference Tuesday, Feb. 14, 2023 announcing that he is the new Indianapolis Colts Head Coach. Colts Owner and CEO Jim Irsay and General Manager Chris Ballard introduced the new coach in the Gridiron Hall of the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center. Shane Steichen Is The New Indianapolis Colts Head Coach | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Indianapolis Colts are at home to take on the Tennessee Titans for week 6 of the 2026 season, kickoff is at 1:00 p.m. EST. Last week we saw the Colts march into Pittsburgh and helped Aaron Rodgers turn back the clock, made sure he looked much younger than his 42 years would suggest. The game wasn’t close. At no point did it feel like the Colts could control much of anything. This Colts defense is amongst the worst of the last decade and there is very little hope they’ll be able to do much of anything to improve it, markedly, this season. It’s bad. Offensively, Daniel Jones didn’t turn the ball over. That’s good. But it’s only noteworthy because he turned the ball over seven (7) times in the teams first four games. Improvement it always a good thing but in this case the bar was pretty low. Side Note: I told you about this last week but I’m probably going to keep reminding you each week because I think it’s important for everyone who enjoys these gameday threads. The SB Nation app makes commenting, especially in these game feeds, so much easier. At this point I roll my eyes every time someone asks me to download another app, but this one really does improve the experience so much that even I am telling you that if you like to hang out here, chat, celebrate, commiserate, and argue in the comments, this app is actually worth your time. Links are directly below. Join Stampede Blue on game day! Stay on top of every Colts update and debate every snap with other diehard fans. Game-day discussion is smoother in the SB Nation app. Fewer ads Jump easily between conversations Faster commenting and posting Download on iOS or Android . Despite the collective pessimism surrounding this team, the Colts are a better team than the Titans (another very low bar). They should absolutely win this game. If by some chance we see Indy lose today, in my opinion, it seals the fate of everyone in the Colts front office. I’m less sold on the coaching staff being let go, for a multitude of reasons, but anything is possible. As things currently stand, to save their jobs, the Colts might have to win out and go on a playoff run, anyway. And no one can envision anything like that happening at this point. Today I expect the Titans offense to put up points but I expect the Indy offense to look better than they have, maybe better than at any point this season. Titans head coach Robert Saleh talked at length during a press conference this week about the complexity of his defensive system and how difficult it is, how long it takes players to fully understand and the benefits he expects to see once everyone is up to speed. He acknowledged they were still working through things and it’s pretty obvious that defense isn’t up to speed yet. Hopefully we can see the Colts offense move the ball on the ground. So far Indy hasn’t had any answers for the stacked boxes Jonathan Taylor has faced. Tight end Tyler Warren hurt his groin on Friday and is questionable to play today, which is very concerning. Hopefully Josh Downs is feeling good because this offense is going to need him. Prediction: Titans: 24 Colts: 30 As always, go Colts. title: Jaguars Winners And Losers From Week 6: Mistakes Finally Catch Up
summary: The pendulum finally swung the other way and it actually cost the Jacksonville Jaguars this time. After a few weeks of close shaves, the Jags slipped in a winnable game, falling to the Houston Texas 37-34 in London Sunday morning. Jacksonville overcame a 10-point fourth quarter deficit but chose a long field goal instead of […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 18: Bhayshul Tuten of the Jacksonville Jaguars celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the NFL London Series match between Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium on October 18, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Alex Davidson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The pendulum finally swung the other way and it actually cost the Jacksonville Jaguars this time. After a few weeks of close shaves, the Jags slipped in a winnable game, falling to the Houston Texas 37-34 in London Sunday morning . Jacksonville overcame a 10-point fourth quarter deficit but chose a long field goal instead of going for it which gave the Texans back the ball and most importantly an AFC South victory. This loss was by no means one of those losses where it feels like the world is falling apart but it does sting because it was so winnable. If not for a few drops, a phantom holding call or even just one more field goal attempt, the Jags could basically have already clinched a playoff spot. Instead, Jacksonville goes into its bye week with a loss and plenty of time to ponder it. WINNERS Travis Hunter While the loss was brutal, there was plenty of good that happened on the beat up field in Wembley. Notably, Travis Hunter came alive on both sides of the ball. Hunter scored his second ever offensive touchdown, which both have now come in England, on nine snaps of offense. He caught four passes for 59 yards in total. On defense, he recorded what seemed like a game-saving pick in the end zone. TRAVIS HUNTER PICKS IT OFF IN THE END ZONE HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/3t5alPW3z1 — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Overall, he became the fourth player ever with a pick and an offensive touchdown in one game since the NFL merger. Sunday morning’s showing from Hunter was the exact reason the Jags moved up to get him. While it hasn’t always played out like it did against the Texans, the proof of concept was there. Lining Hunter up in the backfield and having him cut hard across the middle of the field behind the linebackers was beautiful to see. Real bad day for the Hunter haters after this one. WE ARE WITNESSING GREATNESS: Jacksonville #Jaguars two-way superstar Travis Hunter has been DOMINATING at both wide receiver and cornerback today. Travis Hunter’s stats so far: • 4 targets • 4 receptions • 59 receiving yards • 1 touchdown • 1 interception • 3 tackles •… — MLFootball (@MLFootball) October 18, 2026 Bhayshul Tuten Another solid offensive performance came from running back Bhayshul Tuten, who did literally all he could running and catching the ball to try and will the Jags to victory. Tuten only had 39 yards on the ground, but anyone who watched the game saw those were hard, thumping yards. He also caught four passes for 48 yards and two scores. Sunday was his first multi-score game of his career. Last year, Tuten had just two touchdown catches over the course of the season but matched that Sunday. With his evolving pass catching ability, it makes more and more sense why the Jags handed him the keys to the RB1 spot this past offseason. Tuten did split usage with Chris Rodgriguez (11 carries, 55 yards) but the two made a perfectly fine tandem. The Jags eclipsed 100 yards rushing between the pair, showing that the coaches and Trevor Lawrence have faith in either back to get the dirty work done. Had it not been for that holding call (get used to hearing about that) Tuten might have had a hattrick. Bhayshul Tuten weaves his way in for the touchdown and the @Jaguars are on the board HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/oBswI5s9Mr — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 The Offensive Line Maybe the best offensive day of all was had by the offensive line. What a freaking day by the likes of Walker Little and Cole Van Lanen who helped blank the Houston defensive line for zero sacks. Houston came into Sunday recording sacks in every game it had played, totalling 18. That number didn’t grow after playing the Jags, much to the surprise of everyone. Maybe the field conditions and slipping had something to do with it but no matter. Outside of a few hurries on Lawrence, Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson Jr. were a non-factor in the pass rush game. That is absolutely how you win games. You stopped the best defensive line tandem in football and rushed for over 100 yards and passed for over 300. Talk about a winning formula. Huge credit to Little for getting his first start of the year like that and helping to put up a goose egg in the sack category. James Gladstone Piggybacking off the Hunter point, James Gladstone gets a nod for his recent draft picks playing well against the Texans. Obviously Hunter is the big story, and deservedly so, but he wasn’t the only one. Rookie tight end Nate Boerkircher caught his first career touchdown in eye-popping fashion Sunday to hopefully silence the haters on the “reach” of that draft pick. Fellow tight end Tanner Koizol played sparingly, but had a solid block on Hunter’s big gain of 24-yards. Rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon continued to start and helped the line to its no sack day. And Gladstone was also the guy that drafted Tuten and signed Rodriguez Jr. Gladstone signing Jakobi Meyers led the team in receiving with five catches for 83 yards. When was the last time we had the general manager of the Jacksonville Jaguars on the winners list? Now he just needs to cook up a trade for number seven. Nate Boerkircher with the INSANE one-handed touchdown catch! HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/oBhAyPowx9 — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 LOSERS Brian Thomas Jr. Speaking of number seven, it’s got to be close to over for Brian Thomas Jr.’s time in Jacksonville. After a couple key drops and literally no snaps played in the second half, Thomas is becoming far more of a hindrance than an addition for this offense. Coupled with Josh Cameron coming on as a true wide receiver (shoutout Gladstone) Thomas makes no more sense on this roster. Much like the Texans trading for Marvin Harrison Jr. to give that wide receiver a new chance at success, the same has got to be done for Thomas. The third-year receiver hasn’t recorded a catch in two straight games. Both his drops – while maybe not on the prettiest balls ever thrown by Lawrence – were still big time drops. He cost the team again Sunday. It has to come to a time when enough is enough. This past game probably was that. Asked #Jaguars coach Liam Coen if it will be tough to show confidence in WR Brian Thomas Jr. (no snaps in second half): "Guys have to step up and make plays.” Says everything doesn't it? — Ryan O'Halloran (@ryanohalloran) October 18, 2026 Liam Coen This is now two straight weeks where you can point the blame in some capacity at the head coach for his execution of scoring situations. The red zone offense wasn’t the issue like it was last week, it was the decision making on when or when not to try to score more points. The drives that really stick out are: Electing to punt on the team’s opening drive, opting out of a field goal well shorter than the 60-yarder to tie the game late. Going for it on fourth-and-3 on the 37 and not getting it, leading to a Texans touchdown at the end of the first quarter. Kicking that 60-yarder which gave the Texans the ball back with three timeouts and a chance to win the game. Coen can’t be blamed for that holding call which led to Lawrence’s pick, but leaving a handful of points on the board in a game that was decided by a field goal is glaring. He also maybe gets a bit of egg on his face for not using Hunter more over someone like Thomas after what we saw from Hunter Sunday. Coen has done so much good, but sometimes his game management seems questionable. Game management seems to be a plague all over all of the NFL but Coen is certainly suffering from it. As was said last week, it’s not solely on Coen. He can’t go out and catch the ball. He can’t prevent weird penalties or even sack the…
author: Henry Zimmer

title: Three reasons why the Jaguars lost to the Texans
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars had every opportunity to extend their winning streak to four games, but a familiar divisional rival had other ideas. Houston Texans kicker Ka’imi Fairbairn drilled a 49-yard field goal as time expired to seal a dramatic 34-31 victory at Wembley Stadium, leaving Jacksonville to reflect on a game in which costly mistakes […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 18: Ka'imi Fairbairn of the Houston Texans celebrates after kicking the winning field goal in the fourth quarter during the NFL London Series match between Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium on October 18, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Alex Davidson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars had every opportunity to extend their winning streak to four games, but a familiar divisional rival had other ideas. Houston Texans kicker Ka’imi Fairbairn drilled a 49-yard field goal as time expired to seal a dramatic 34-31 victory at Wembley Stadium, leaving Jacksonville to reflect on a game in which costly mistakes and defensive lapses proved decisive. Trevor Lawrence threw four touchdown passes, Travis Hunter delivered a historic performance on both sides of the ball, and Cam Little connected from 60 yards to force a tie late in the fourth quarter. Yet none of it was enough to overcome a Texans offense that consistently found answers when it needed them most. Here are three reasons why the Jaguars came up short in London. Run defense runs out of steam The cutback and vision from Jawhar Jordan on this touchdown run 🔥 HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/xRtD213b8j — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Jacksonville’s defensive front had established itself as a major strength during the opening weeks of the season, but Houston exposed its vulnerability at a critical point in Sunday’s contest. The Texans entered the fourth quarter with a 31-21 advantage after Jawhar Jordan broke through for a 25-yard touchdown run with just 50 seconds remaining in the third period. The play was particularly damaging because Jacksonville had just allowed the Texans to convert a third down without having to make a conventional defensive stop. Cornerback Jarrian Jones was flagged for pass interference on third-and-four, giving Houston a fresh set of downs and moving the ball into scoring territory. Jordan made the Jaguars pay immediately, finding a crease in the defense and racing into the end zone to restore a 10-point lead. Woody Marks also helped Houston establish a more balanced offensive attack, while quarterback C.J. Stroud ensured the Jaguars couldn’t simply focus on stopping the run. The combination kept Jacksonville guessing and made it increasingly difficult to get off the field on third down. The Jaguars deserve credit for battling back into the contest, but the defensive front needed to make a stand when Houston had the opportunity to take control. Instead, Jordan’s touchdown left Jacksonville facing another uphill climb, and it took a remarkable fourth-quarter effort just to get back on level terms. For a defense that had helped propel the Jaguars into the AFC South lead, this was a disappointing time to lose its grip on the line of scrimmage – particularly against an offense that had, until this point, failed to move the ball effectively all year. Penalties and explosive plays the difference Jaylin Noel sold this route so well 😮‍💨 HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/qCpVInbmD1 — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Jacksonville’s defensive problems extended beyond the running game. Stroud completed 24 of 34 passes for 312 yards and three touchdowns, repeatedly punishing the Jaguars whenever their coverage broke down or the defense handed Houston an extra opportunity. Jaylin Noel was a particularly troublesome matchup. The Texans wide receiver finished with a career-high 107 receiving yards and a touchdown, including a crucial 50-yard reception with 48 seconds remaining in the first half. That completion immediately put Houston in scoring position, and Stroud found tight end Foster Moreau for a one-yard touchdown with just eight seconds left before halftime. The damage was significant. Jacksonville had taken a 14-10 lead when Lawrence connected with running back Bhayshul Tuten for a two-yard touchdown, but the defense surrendered the advantage before the break. Rather than heading into halftime in front, the Jaguars went into the locker room trailing 17-14. The problems continued after halftime. A too-many-men-on-the-field penalty on a Houston punt extended a Texans possession, and Noel subsequently caught a 13-yard touchdown pass to make it 24-14. Later, Jones’ pass interference penalty helped set up Jordan’s touchdown run. Those errors turned manageable situations into scoring opportunities. The Jaguars weren’t simply beaten by spectacular individual plays; they repeatedly gave Houston additional chances to move the chains and capitalize. There was a late redemption moment when Hunter intercepted Stroud in the end zone, but even that outstanding play couldn’t erase the earlier damage. Jacksonville had forced Houston into enough difficult situations to compete, yet its inability to close out drives ultimately proved decisive. Too many points left on the field A "holding" call on Breton Strange wiped a Jaguars TD off the board 😩 Did the refs get this right? *Disclaimer* We're on Jacksonville to win 🫠 pic.twitter.com/GMCqpAzYks — Covers.com Football (@Covers_Football) October 18, 2026 Lawrence’s four touchdown passes make it difficult to argue that Jacksonville’s offense was the primary reason for the defeat. The quarterback threw for 306 yards, connected with Tuten twice, found rookie tight end Nate Boerkircher for his first NFL touchdown, and later linked up with Hunter to keep the Jaguars in contention. However, an early sequence demonstrated how quickly a promising possession could unravel. Jacksonville appeared to have taken control of a drive when Tuten found the end zone on a rushing attempt, only for a holding penalty on tight end Brenton Strange to wipe out the score. The Jaguars were left to start again, and Lawrence subsequently threw an end-zone interception to Houston cornerback Kamari Lassiter. Instead of putting points on the board, Jacksonville came away empty-handed. The penalty and turnover were particularly frustrating because the offense had already done the difficult work of moving into scoring territory. The Jaguars eventually found their rhythm, and Lawrence’s four touchdown passes kept them within striking distance throughout the afternoon. But in a game decided by three points, throwing away a scoring opportunity carries enormous consequences. A touchdown on that early drive would have changed the complexion of the contest and potentially altered the way Houston approached the remainder of the first half. Jacksonville’s offense did enough to give the team a chance to win, but it couldn’t afford to squander opportunities against a divisional opponent capable of matching its scoring output. The final blow The Jaguars’ comeback deserved admiration. Hunter’s fourth-quarter touchdown brought Jacksonville within three points, and his subsequent interception gave the offense another chance to rescue the game. Little then delivered a spectacular 60-yard field goal with 1:55 remaining to tie the score at 31-31. Yet Houston still had time to respond. And respond they did. For Jacksonville, the defeat was a reminder that a strong offensive performance cannot always compensate for defensive breakdowns and self-inflicted mistakes. The Jaguars had the talent and resilience to fight back, but they couldn’t make the decisive stop when it mattered most. Sunday’s defeat was almost the polar opposite of the first London leg, where a stuttering offense was bailed out by special teams in a game the Jags should have lost. This week, their luck ran out. The loss snapped a three-game winning streak and left Jacksonville at 4-2 heading into its bye week. The Jaguars remain firmly in the AFC South picture, but their performance at Wembley provided a clear list of issues to address before their next game.
author: Simon Carroll

title: Jaguars Stunned in London: Texans Offense Takes Over
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars struggled to contain the Houston Texans’ offense in London, suffering a frustrating loss to their AFC South rival. Jacksonville entered the matchup with an opportunity to strengthen its position in the division, but Houston found ways to exploit the Jaguars’ defense and make life difficult throughout the contest. Now, the Jaguars are […]
full_text: Oct 18, 2026; London, ENG; Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Travis Hunter (12) reacts during the second half against the Houston Texans at Wembley Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Jacksonville Jaguars struggled to contain the Houston Texans’ offense in London, suffering a frustrating loss to their AFC South rival. Jacksonville entered the matchup with an opportunity to strengthen its position in the division, but Houston found ways to exploit the Jaguars’ defense and make life difficult throughout the contest. Now, the Jaguars are left searching for answers as they look to regroup, address their shortcomings, and get back on track. As the Jaguars fall to 4-2 heading into the Week 7 bye week, here’s everything you need to know from Jacksonville’s Week 6 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans to wrap up the Jaguars’ 2026 International slate. Post-game notables: Early Mistakes Hurt Jacksonville Jacksonville headed into halftime down three following a first half that featured four dropped passes (two by Brian Thomas Jr., one by Parker Washington, and one by Jakobi Meyers). Each Thomas drop cost the Jaguars a field goal opportunity. The Parker Washington drop would have resulted in Jacksonville being in field goal range and a red zone Lawrence interception after a bad holding call cost them a first-half touchdown. In total, Jacksonville mistakes (or bad penalties) cost a total of 16 first-half points, with the team down 17-14 at halftime. While the team ended the day with just six penalties, four of them came in the opening half and cost the team in a tight matchup. WR Travis Hunter Arrives The Jaguars’ 9-play, 61-yard, fourth-quarter touchdown drive featured a touchdown from the dual-threat Hunter. Liam Coen consistently used Hunter to find the prime matchup, bringing in a show-stopping three catches for 40 yards. title: 5 things we learned from the Chiefs’ Week 6 victory over the Chargers
summary: Coming off the bye, the Kansas City Chiefs entered this game looking to go 3-0 against AFC West opponents this season. It was evident from the jump who the better team was. The Chiefs didn’t play a perfect game, and at times it felt like they were coasting, but they dominated all four quarters. Kansas […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Coming off the bye, the Kansas City Chiefs entered this game looking to go 3-0 against AFC West opponents this season. It was evident from the jump who the better team was. The Chiefs didn’t play a perfect game, and at times it felt like they were coasting, but they dominated all four quarters. Kansas City’s pass rushers and standout running back Kenneth Walker III were especially impressive in the Chiefs’ 22-6 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers . Here are five things we learned from the Chiefs stealing the Chargers’ lunch money: 1. K9 is not just the top dog; he’s the NFL MVP Through the first six weeks of the season, this isn’t even up for debate. I know the NFL decided in some nefarious back-channel meeting that the NFL MVP is now a quarterback award. The only exception is when a running back is having a truly transcendent year—well, Kenneth Walker III is doing just that. Over five games, Walker has 665 rushing yards and averages 6.2 yards per carry, with eight total touchdowns. For reference, the last time a non-quarterback won the NFL MVP was in 2012 when Minnesota Vikings running back Adrian Peterson won the award. That season, Peterson rushed for 2,097 yards and 13 total touchdowns, averaging six yards per carry. Before Peterson won the award, you have to go back to 2006 to find the next season a non-quarterback won the MVP. Chargers running back LaDainian Tomlinson won that year. Interestingly, in 2005, Seattle Seahawks running back Shaun Alexander also won MVP. In 2006, Tomlinson ran for 1,815 yards and 31 total touchdowns, averaging 5.2 yards per carry. In 2005, Alexander ran 1,880 yards and 28 total touchdowns, averaging 5.1 yards per carry. It’s still early, and Walker needs to keep up this pace and stay healthy for the rest of the season, but right now, Walker is on pace to rush for 2,260 yards and 27 total touchdowns. Those numbers would not only surpass Peterson’s 2012 MVP campaign, but also beat Los Angeles Rams Eric Dickerson’s all-time single-season rushing record of 2,105 yards that has stood since 1984. Even more impressive. He’s on pace for 2,583 all-purpose yards, which would also beat Tennessee Titans running back Chris Johnson’s 2009 record of 2,509 yards, Walker isn’t just on pace for a great season; he’s on pace for the greatest season of any running back in NFL history. Kenneth Walker III kept rolling with another huge game for Kansas City. 19 CAR, 128 RUSH YDS, 6.7 YPC, 2 TD, 2 REC, 11 REC YDS Walker continues to build a serious OPOY case in his first season with the Chiefs. pic.twitter.com/H7UDopZeHW https://t.co/g2cWBUkgRc — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) October 18, 2026 2. Chiefs are the Kings of the West It feels good to be back on the throne. With this victory over the Chargers, the Chiefs have ensured they will have at least a .500 record against AFC West opponents this season. With the Las Vegas Raiders losing to the Buffalo Bills , the Raiders are 3-3, and the Denver Broncos are the Chiefs’ next closest opponents at 4-2. But let’s be honest: after watching Bo Nix’s ineptitude and the rest of Denver’s offense, do you really think they have what it takes to catch up with the Chiefs? As for the Chargers, they look like the worst team in the NFL. No, they look worse than bad. They look cursed. Sports have a long history of cursed franchises. The reasons a franchise might be cursed range from how fans treat it to trading a legendary player. In the Chargers case, I’m going to jump to an unfounded conclusion and say it’s because they left San Diego. They are being punished from the great beyond by a spirit who is angry they relocated to Los Angeles. San Diego loved that franchise, and they left it for the bright lights of Hollywood. The only question is, whose spirit is responsible for tormenting them? Personally, as a Chiefs fan, I hope it’s Marty Schottenheimer. 3. Nikko Remigio is not as dependable as we were told We were told Nikko Remigio was the Chiefs’ kick and punt returner because he was dependable and does not put the ball on the ground. Well, that changed in this game. He fumbled once and nearly fumbled again, but he was saved because he was down by a hair. The Chiefs also had a block in the back on the play where Remigio fumbled. Harrison Butker missed a point-after attempt and has only made 25% of his attempts from 50+ yards. It doesn’t matter if you can kick the ball a mile if you can’t kick it straight. Not a great day for Harrison Butker. Good from 44, misses wide right from 52, and missed a PAT. — Matt Derrick (@mattderrick) October 18, 2026 4. A bad offensive line makes your pass rush look awesome Chiefs edge rusher George Karlaftis brought his hardhat and lunchpail to work today, and proceeded to abuse the Chargers’ battered offensive line. In fact, nearly everyone joined in on the fun of bullying the human-shaped cutouts the Chargers propped up in front of Justin Herbert. Ashton Gillotte, Peter Woods, and Felix Anudike-Uzomah all hit the quarterback. And just like their last game against the Raiders, when the Chiefs needed somebody to step up and close out the game, the pass rush showed up, with R Mason Thomas beating his man around the edge and hitting Justin Herbert’s arm as he threw. Chiefs edge rushers today: – George Karlaftis: 26.3% pressure rate, 2.33 time to pressure, 1 sack, 2 TFLs – R Mason Thomas: 20.8% pressure rate, 2.31 time to pressure — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) October 19, 2026 5. The Chiefs need Josh Simmons Not because the offensive line played bad today. On the contrary, I thought it was one of their better games this season. But they also took their lumps. Right tackle Jaylon Moore left the game with a concussion. Left guard Suamataia had a calf stinger. Diego Pounds has been inactive all season. But even if fully healthy, the Chiefs didn’t have much depth on the offensive line. Despite playing admirably, I don’t feel great about the Chiefs running out Kahlil Benson and Joshua Ezeudu for a full four quarters against the Seahawks next week. Trying to tackle Kenneth Walker does NOT look fun pic.twitter.com/FtfvsQo2g1 — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) October 4, 2026

summary: The Kansas City Chiefs keep winning, and the latest in five consecutive victories to start this season put quarterback Patrick Mahomes in rarefied air. When asked during his post-game press conference, Mahomes joked about Brady’s incredible success. “My honest first reaction is […]
full_text: (Photo by Matthew J. Lee/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs keep winning, and the latest in five consecutive victories to start this season put quarterback Patrick Mahomes in rarefied air. He tied all-time quarterback Tom Brady for fastest to reach 100 career wins. When asked during his post-game press conference, Mahomes joked about Brady’s incredible success. “My honest first reaction is they’ve said this from 97 on. I’m like, ‘When did (QB) Tom (Brady) lose another game?’” Mahomes said to laughter from the press pool. “Because I feel every game I win, I tie him.” Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device! For Apple devices, click here . For Android devices, click here . The latest Kansas City Chiefs news Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes Ties Tom Brady’s All-Time Record in Chargers Win | Heavy Sports Mahomes earned the 100th victory of his career on Sunday, October 18 against the visiting Los Angeles Chargers, joining Brady as the youngest QBs to hit that major milestone. “I mean, it’s awesome. Because, I mean, he’s the GOAT, man,” Mahomes said in an on-field, postgame interview with CBS Sports reporter Melanie Collins. “He’s the one that has kinda shown us how to do it in winning the Super Bowls and winning every single week. So it’s always an honor if you’re mentioned in his name. But it seems like every time I win a game, I’m tying him, so I’m gonna keep winning.” The Chiefs are 5-0 — and their offense may be returning to their dynastic heights | NBC News The last time Kansas City started 5-0 was in the 2024 season, when it finished the regular season 11-0 in one-score games and white-knuckled two playoff wins before getting blown out by the Philadelphia Eagles in the Super Bowl. But this is an entirely different 5-0, as the Chiefs are now powered by a highly efficient offense and a capable defense. While Kansas City has been a perennial title contender under Mahomes, this year’s team is much more formidable than it was the last few seasons. Roughing-the-passer call on the Chiefs upsets Andy Reid, fans and rules analyst | The Kansas City Star Defensive end Ashton Gillotte was flagged for roughing the passer when he ran into Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert. That flag wiped out an interception by the Chiefs’ Chris Rolland-Wallace. “To me,” Steratore said, “I just didn’t like the foul for roughing the passer.” Steratore noted Gillotte tried to avoid contact and didn’t throw his body at Herbert. Fortunately for the Chiefs, they ended up getting an interception later in the drive when linebacker Jack Cochrane picked off Herbert. ‘None of that matters’ – Nick Wright gives ‘dumb’ Kansas City Chiefs verdict after comfortable win | HITC “The Chiefs did literally everything you’re supposed to do to lose a dumb game. They missed an extra point, had a special teams turnover, threw a pick in the end zone & got stuffed at the 1. But, luckily, they were playing the Chargers so none of that matters,” the First Things First star wrote on X. Chiefs defensive back ejected for punching Chargers player | KSHB 41 Initially, both Roland-Wallace and Harkey were called for offsetting personal foul penalties on the first play of the final period. But after an expedited league review, referee Alan Eck announced that Roland-Wallace was ejected for “landing a punch,” leading to jeers inside Arrowhead Stadium. Roland-Wallace, a versatile third-year defensive back from USC, had four tackles, including one for a loss, before the ejection. Around the NFL C.J. Gardner-Johnson apologizes after getting ejected for spitting at Brock Bowers | The Athletic “My passion and competitive nature have always been a huge part of who I am, but I also understand that there is a line that should never be crossed,” Gardner-Johnson posted on his Instagram story. “The gesture I made toward my opponent was inappropriate, unnecessary, and not a reflection of the respect I have for him or this game. “There is no excuse for my actions, and I take full accountability. No matter how emotional or intense the competition gets, I have to hold myself to a higher standard.” Harbaugh mum on McDaniel, says Chargers need ‘to address everything’ | ESPN “I don’t know,” Herbert said on what hasn’t clicked for him in this offense so far. “If I had the answers, then we’d definitely be having a different conversation.” Harbaugh tried his best to explain what he saw from his quarterback Sunday, saying Herbert “didn’t have a lot of chances” and did everything he could possibly do. However, the coach again mentioned that what the Chargers are doing in preparation is not showing up during games. “Just one of the things that’s not translating from meetings, practice to the game,” Harbaugh said. “Our run game, our passing game, our short-yardage game. Being able to move the ball and score points, whether that’s in the red zone or if we have the ball at the 1 or the 40 or the 50. What’s not translating? How do we get it to translate?” Has the Travis Hunter breakout arrived? Jacksonville CB/WR showcases long-term, two-way potential vs. Texans | CBS Sports Hunter is now the first player with a receiving touchdown and an interception in the same game since Pro Football Hall of Famer Brian Dawkins did so back in 2022, also against the Texans. Hunter’s performance on Sunday is now just the fourth time a player has produced a receiving touchdown and an interception in the same game (including the playoffs) since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Xavier Worthy rises to the occasion for Chiefs’ offense They told me all week: it’s going to be for me,” Worthy said. “I have to step up for the receiving room; guys are down, and I did my one of 11.” “It’s obviously great to be targeted early and often… getting your feel for the game.” It was a slower pace to the finish line in Kansas City’s 22-6 win over Los Angeles on offense, but Worthy still finished as the team’s leader in receptions (7), receiving yards (73) and yards after catch (43). He caught all seven passes thrown his way and moved the chains four times. title: 9 Winners and 4 Losers from the Chiefs’ win over the Chargers
summary: Your 5-0 Kansas City Chiefs beat the Los Angeles Chargers 22-6 at Arrowhead Stadium, outgaining them 422-259 and, most importantly, keeping Los Angeles out of the end zone. The pass rush showed up, the Chiefs forced two turnovers and every time the Chargers had an opportunity to make this a game, Kansas City’s defense shut […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Your 5-0 Kansas City Chiefs beat the Los Angeles Chargers 22-6 at Arrowhead Stadium, outgaining them 422-259 and, most importantly, keeping Los Angeles out of the end zone. The pass rush showed up, the Chiefs forced two turnovers and every time the Chargers had an opportunity to make this a game, Kansas City’s defense shut the door. It wasn’t perfect. Kansas City turned it over twice, missed two kicks, couldn’t gain a yard when it really needed one and committed eight penalties. But the Chiefs also controlled the game from beginning to end. Here are a few Chiefs who stood out against the Chargers — for better or worse. 9 Winners Wide receiver Xavier Worthy : There was no 60-yard bomb or trick play that asked Worthy to outrun the field. In this game, Worthy caught all seven targets for 73 yards, becoming Mahomes’ most reliable wide receiver with Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton unavailable. Tight ends Noah Gray, Travis Kelce, and Jake Briningstool: The Chiefs got contributions from all three tight ends on Sunday afternoon. Kelce fought through an ankle injury to continue his great start, while Noah Gray had a big catch-and-run. Together, they caught 7 of 8 targets for 106 yards (53 each)—much of it YAC. You won’t see Briningstool on the box score, but he delivered key blocks on some of the biggest running plays of the afternoon. Tight end is a critical position group for a running team, especially one with question marks at wide receiver, and it’s encouraging to see all three get involved. Running Back Kenneth Walker: On 3rd and 1, Kenneth Walker broke free for 33 yards and a touchdown. He finished with 21 touches and nearly 140 total yards. He’s not only leading the NFL in rushing in 2026, but he’s already surpassed the Chiefs’ leading rusher from 2025– in just five games. He’s explosive. He breaks tackles. He makes people miss. And maybe the most surprising stat: Andy Reid seems willing to keep giving him the football. EDGE George Karlaftis: Give credit to the pass rush as a whole– they just doubled their sack total on the season; they’re still getting a lot of pressure… and they also got home this week. The combination works– R Mason Thomas’s speed, the relentless effort of Ashton Gillotte, the physical force that is Chris Jones, along with Steve Spagnuolo’s blitz packages. But the most impressive individual effort came from George Karlaftis once again– three QB hits, two tackles for loss, two batted passes, and a sack. Furious George is on a tear. Wide receiver Cyrus Allen: The true breakout game hasn’t happened yet, but Allen showed some great signs of life again this week. He caught both his targets against the Chargers, and his role should keep growing. Cornerback Nohl Williams: His ball skills are as remarkable as his tenacity. Nohl defended two more passes and got some great coverage reps. He also had a tackle for loss, attacking running backs and receivers on screen plays with no fear. Linebacker Jack Cochrane: We bag on Cochrane most weeks, so it’s only fair to give him credit for what could have been one of the biggest plays of Sunday’s game. Under heavy pressure, Chargers QB Justin Herbert threw a pass right to #43. To his credit, Jack Cochrane not only secured the interception but also returned it 48 yards, setting up the offense in the red zone. It’s not his fault that Mahomes gave it right back with an endzone pick of his own. 4 Losers Return specialist Nikko Remigio: Dave Toub raves about Remigio’s ability to catch a punt and be reliable. Well, today he fumbled a punt and almost fumbled another on a kickoff. Maybe we could overlook a lapse now and then if they were also making huge plays, flipping the field, or even scoring now and then. But they aren’t. Kicker Harrison Butker: Like Remigio, Butker’s only real job is to be reliable. Once again, he missed a field goal and an extra point. Once again, it didn’t matter– but it will at some point. Have we mentioned lately that Harrison Butker is among the game’s highest-paid kickers? The short-yardage offense: Blame the offensive line, the predictable playcalling, the nose tackle fullback, or all of the above. The Chiefs were stuffed on fourth-and-goal from the 1 on Sunday, the third consecutive game Walker has been stopped on a fourth-and-short run. The Andy Reid-led offense, which averaged 7.4 yards per play Sunday, shouldn’t have had this much trouble gaining three feet. Convert a couple more of these, and this game would have been a massive blowout. Center Creed Humphrey: The best center in the game was undoubtedly a big part of the run game’s success, but the low snap issue reared its ugly head again this week. I’m sure it’ll get worked out, but against a good team, it could have been costly. Note: Applying the labels “losers” is not meant to be a judgment on the talent or character of any of these individuals. It’s just a simple way to grade their job performance in a single game. No disrespect is intended.
author: Matt Stagner

title: Kenneth Walker continues to lead Chiefs’ offense with masterful running
summary: Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker has made it a weekly tradition to surpass the already-high expectations of Chiefs Kingdom. If he didn’t blow our minds enough by gashing the Denver Broncos for 173 yards on the ground in the season opener, he doubled down against the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 4 with […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker has made it a weekly tradition to surpass the already-high expectations of Chiefs Kingdom. If he didn’t blow our minds enough by gashing the Denver Broncos for 173 yards on the ground in the season opener, he doubled down against the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 4 with 177 yards and a 76-yard run that turned the game in the second half. Coming out of the bye week, there was reasonable speculation that rookie running back Emmett Johnson would spell Walker to keep the talented lead back fresh. Instead, Walker took the load again, gaining 139 yards from scrimmage on 21 touches. None of his carries matched the long touchdown run that gave the Chiefs an early 9-0 lead over the Los Angeles Chargers . Counter blocked to absolute perfection. Play side double team ✅ Kick out block ✅ Lead puller seals the LB ✅ K9 breaking arm tackles ✅✅ pic.twitter.com/hmskKX5k1C — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 19, 2026 On third-and-1, quarterback Patrick Mahomes came out of an under-center formation to hand off to Walker off counter action; right guard Trey Smith and second-year tight end Jake Briningstool made the key blocks to spring him in the first quarter. “The 33-yarder was pretty open,” Walker said in his post-game press conference. “(Tight end) Jake (Briningstool) came across and kicked out; there left was open.” The Chiefs’ lead playmaker credited his teammates for the setup, but head coach Andy Reid understands how much Walker’s talent adds to a well-blocked play. “He knows how to run the ball and knows how to set up runs,” Reid said at the podium following the win. “There’s an art to that and a patience that you’ve got to have and vision and all those things that the great ones have. So, he’s got all of that. And he’s tough. He’s a tough kid.” Mahomes could just stand back and watch Walker paint a masterpiece every time he touches the ball, but that’s not in the two-time MVP’s nature. The quarterback sometimes forgets what position he plays when Walker weaves through the defensive line. Stop if you've heard this before. Kenneth Walker III scored a TD. LACvsKC on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/4ddKGE4RRp — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 That showed on Walker’s two-yard touchdown run late in the first half. “With Kenneth, you’ve got to be ready because he tries to press the front. Every once in a while, he bounces out,” Mahomes explained after the game. “And the defense that they had the moment you got stuffed in that front side, I was like, ‘That guy, if I get him, he’s going to score.” And so, I didn’t get a lot, but I got enough, and so we were able to get him into the end zone and get the big touchdown.” “The first guy never tackles him,” Mahomes elaborated. “I know that guy isn’t going to get him. And just knowing him, and how much of a playmaker he is, he’s going to give it a chance. He’s going to bounce it to either front side or back side. And so, I just put myself in position that if he were going to bounce it back side, I could just give him a step because that guy was there for that reason.” The veteran gunslinger is finding all sorts of ways to contribute to the team’s new run-dominant offense, even leading Walker to the run lanes he doesn’t see yet. “Even in training camp, he usually sees the cutback before I do,” Walker told reporters. “Then he’ll go down and block the guy. That’s really unselfish.” That’s all well and good, but Walker has shown that his talent doesn’t need the extra block from his $500 million quarterback. According to NFL Next Gen Stats , Walker is still the NFL leader in forced missed tackles (52), despite most of the league playing an extra game. Walker’s 128-yard performance also produced some fun stats, marking the fourth time he’s run for at least 117 yards on the ground in a game this season. Share your favorite Walker stat you’ve seen in “The Feed.” An all-time discussion is also brewing in “The Feed,” a week after our Maurice Elston highlighted Walker’s four-game start as among the best in franchise history. However you want to talk about Walker, it’s a fun time to do so! Next up: his revenge game against the Seattle Seahawks on “Sunday Night Football” in Week 7.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Andy Reid gives 4 Chiefs injury updates after Sunday’s win
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs stayed unbeaten with a 22-6 Sunday victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. Several Chiefs players were seen getting attention from the trainers, notably tight end Travis Kelce having his ankle taped multiple times. The only player that the team officially gave an update on was right tackle Jaylon Moore, who went […]
full_text: Oct 18, 2026; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce (87) rushes and is tackled by Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley (0) during the first quarter at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Kansas City Chiefs stayed unbeaten with a 22-6 Sunday victory over the Los Angeles Chargers . Several Chiefs players were seen getting attention from the trainers, notably tight end Travis Kelce having his ankle taped multiple times. The only player that the team officially gave an update on was right tackle Jaylon Moore, who went into the league’s concussion protocol in the second quarter and was ruled out after halftime. Veteran swing offensive lineman Joshua Ezeudu took over for Moore. “As far as the injuries go,” head coach Andy Reid said after the game, “Jaylon Moore has a concussion. That’s the one that stands out the most. Kelce tweaked his ankle there but continued to play. It might be a little sore tomorrow, but he did a nice job tonight.” Reid also discussed a momentary scare for an already depleted wide receiver corps and discussed left guard Kingsley Suamataia momentarily leaving the field in the fourth quarter in obvious pain. “[Jalen] Royals went into be checked for a concussion, but he was good there,” Reid revealed. “Then, Kingsley got kicked in the calf, but he should be ok.” Reid had no mention of cornerback Nohl Williams, who appeared injured on the Chiefs’ first defensive series but returned to play most of the game. Speaking after Reid, quarterback Patrick Mahomes praised general manager Brett Veach for acquiring the offensive line depth needed to cover multiple injuries. “I think guys have done a great job all year,” the superstar noted, “just being able to be available and be ready. I thought in training camp and at the end of training camp into the regular season that Veach did a great job of bringing in a lot of competition. Guys are ready to step up when their number is called. “With that, as well as how we run the ball and how we’ve been protecting, we’ve been able to keep the offense going. The hope that we obviously continue to build on that and that we can be available and that we can be eight or nine deep on the offensive line. We ten guys that we trust that can go in there and play.”

title: Xavier Worthy rises to the occasion for Chiefs’ offense
summary: With injuries hitting the Kansas City Chiefs’ wide receiver corps ahead of the matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers, third-year wideout Xavier Worthy clearly needed to step up. Our Brandon Kiley wrote about it last week: the Chiefs need Worthy now more than ever. He wasted little time proving that he was ready to rise to […]
full_text: (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images With injuries hitting the Kansas City Chiefs ’ wide receiver corps ahead of the matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers , third-year wideout Xavier Worthy clearly needed to step up. Our Brandon Kiley wrote about it last week : the Chiefs need Worthy now more than ever. He wasted little time proving that he was ready to rise to the occasion against the Chargers. On the first play from scrimmage, quarterback Patrick Mahomes found Worthy running to the right—before he caught the ball and quickly jetted back left and into the middle of the field. Worthy’s intentional, aggressive sprint downfield was a welcome sight (despite tight end Travis Kelce blocking in the back). It was the best he has looked with the ball in his hands all season. Immediately after the big play to open the game, Mahomes threw an off-target pass over the middle to Worthy, who stretched out and snagged the ball for a 15-yard gain. The hot start showcased Worthy coming out of the bye week locked in. He stayed locked in on the football during the team’s second drive. On third-and-2, he ran a crossing pattern that came open for Mahomes to float a pass into. Worthy stuck out just one hand at first, then reached out and stared at the ball through the catch-and-run for 17 yards. Worthy, along with running back Kenneth Walker, became the constant weapon the Chiefs needed in a game where the offense stalled too many times. Kansas City saw two red-zone opportunities end in failure, whether through an avoidable interception by Mahomes or a fourth-and-1 stop in the second half. Before halftime, Worthy caught a pass over the middle and showcased the 4.21-second 40-yard dash across the field and out of bounds, setting up Butker to kick a 50-yard field goal before intermission. In the third quarter, Worthy kept a possession alive by laying out for a quick sideline pass that was wide. The Chiefs didn’t move the chains on third and short, but it was the speedster’s sixth catch of the game on six targets. No other Chiefs receiver had more than one catch to that point. #Chiefs WR Xavier Worthy on increased involvement in the offense today. #Chiefskingdom pic.twitter.com/pKKwPzVENg — 96.5 The Fan (@TheFan965) October 19, 2026 In the locker room after the game, Worthy told local media he was ready for more usage, courtesy of 96.5 the Fan’s post on X . “They told me all week: it’s going to be for me,” Worthy said. “I have to step up for the receiving room; guys are down, and I did my one of 11.” “It’s obviously great to be targeted early and often… getting your feel for the game.” It was a slower pace to the finish line in Kansas City’s 22-6 win over Los Angeles on offense, but Worthy still finished as the team’s leader in receptions (7), receiving yards (73) and yards after catch (43). He caught all seven passes thrown his way and moved the chains four times. He stepped in for Rashee Rice as the high-volume wideout in the Chiefs’ offense and helped generate explosive plays alongside Walker’s positive runs, who led the unit with 128 rushing yards and two touchdowns. The rest of the team’s wideouts combined for five catches for 64 yards. Kansas City has come to expect that impact from Walker, but strong performances from Worthy are nearly just as necessary to keep the offense rolling from here.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Rapid Reaction: Chiefs’ defense keeps lowly Chargers down
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Los Angeles Chargers 22-6 on Sunday afternoon at Arrowhead Stadium, improving their record to 5-0 this season. Here is some rapid reaction to the win: The contest between an undefeated team and a winless team looked the part primarily in one phase of the game: the Chiefs’ defense versus […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Los Angeles Chargers 22-6 on Sunday afternoon at Arrowhead Stadium, improving their record to 5-0 this season. Here is some rapid reaction to the win: The contest between an undefeated team and a winless team looked the part primarily in one phase of the game: the Chiefs’ defense versus the Chargers’ offense. The Chiefs’ offense kept this game close, whether it was conservative fourth-down decisions by head coach Andy Reid early, a red-zone interception by quarterback Patrick Mahomes or a stuffed fourth-and-goal run from inside the one-yard line in the third quarter. Special teams weren’t much help either; after returner Nikko Remigio nearly fumbled the opening kickoff, he fumbled an extended punt return after a three-and-out forced by the Chiefs’ defense inside the Chargers’ own one-yard line. Kicker Harrison Butker also missed a 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter, missing an opportunity to push Kansas City’s lead to 16 points rather than 13 with under 12 minutes to go. Those factors kept the scoreboard from lighting up in the Chiefs’ favor; the Chargers barely sniffed double digits. Los Angeles converted just five of 16 third-down attempts and failed on all three of its fourth-down attempts. Herbert was sacked four times and intercepted once, following an interception that was questionably negated when defensive end Ashton Gillotte came in too high to pressure Herbert as he threw. The Chargers went three-and-out four times and reached double-digit plays on a possession only once before garbage time. Herbert finished with 204 passing yards on 37 attempts and a passer rating of 63.3. That includes a 57-yard bomb to wide receiver Quentin Johnston, completed in incredible fashion despite Chiefs cornerback Mansoor Delane cleanly getting his hands between Johnston’s and disrupting the ball when it first got there. The pass got down to Kansas City’s one-yard line, but the possession ended in a field goal. The Chiefs’ defense held strong, as it did all afternoon. Los Angeles faced third-and-long all game because the Chiefs’ run defense stifled the run game. No Chargers ball carrier gained 10 or more yards on a run; the running backs combined for 43 yards on 16 carries. Linebacker Nick Bolton led the way with 10 tackles, but defensive end George Karlaftis was arguably the most disruptive up front one again. Beyond his six tackles, including two for a loss, Karlaftis batted down two passes and hit Herbert two other times. He didn’t end the Chiefs’ sack drought, however. Gillotte came barreling down on Herbert in the second half, burying him in the grass and drawing a roar from Arrowhead. That was the first of a run on sacks to close the second half; defensive tackles Peter Woods and Chris Jones split a sack on a second-down play in the third quarter when the Chargers were backed up at their own one-yard line. Linebacker Jack Cochrane got in on the action by intercepting a pass and returning it 48 yards down the sideline. Veteran linebacker and former Chargers starter Drue Tranquill pounced on a fumble in the second half. The big men on the Chiefs’ defense had a better effort, but the secondary players highlighted the dominating performance. The injured wide receiver in Los Angeles was limited to just 40 receiving yards, aside from the long-ball completion to Johnston. Cornerback Nohl Williams broke up two passes and made one of the game’s biggest plays when he secured the tackle on a Chargers wideout short of the stick on fourth-and-6. He also recorded a tackle for loss. Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed broke up a pass, forced a fumble, and recorded four tackles. By the end of this AFC West battle, Herbert was walking around gingerly after a quarterback hit by defensive end Felix Anduike-Uzomah. Then safety Chamarri Conner flew through the line of scrimmage and brought Herbert down just before the two-minute warning. It was the third sack of the game and felt like the nail in the coffin of the game and the Chargers’ season — until Karlaftis flew into the backfield and secured the team’s fourth sack of the afternoon. Herbert took nine hits. The 0-6 team found life in the second half after errors by the Chiefs’ offense and special teams, but defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s unit ensured Kansas City coasted to a fifth straight win by the end of the fourth quarter.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just before halftime against the Los Angeles Chargers , the Kansas City Chiefs ’ offense took the field with backup lineman Joshua Ezeudu at right tackle. He manned the position for the three plays that led into kicker Harrison Butker making a 50-yard field goal to put the Chiefs in front at halftime by a score of 19-3. OL Jaylon Moore is in concussion protocol. pic.twitter.com/LRCgi20rxE — Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) October 18, 2026 Moore is in concussion protocol, the team said. That sets up Kansas City to start the second half with Ezeudu, a fifth-year career backup, at right tackle. Later in the third quarter, the team ruled Moore out for the game . Ezeudu has 10 career starts, according to Pro Football-Reference . He has spent most of his NFL career at left tackle or left guard with the New York Giants . Per Pro Football Focus , Ezeudu has 402 snaps at left tackle, 317 snaps at left guard and just 3 snaps at right tackle during his professional career. However, this preseason with the Giants, Ezeudu lined up at right tackle 44 times and right guard another 30 times. With left tackle Josh Simmons (Back) still recovering from injury, Ezeudu is apparently the next man up at offensive tackle after Kansas City traded for he and Diego Pounds (Gameday inactive) before the regular season began.

During the broadcast, it was announced that McConkey would be out for the remainder of the game. So […]
full_text: Los Angeles Chargers wide receiver Ladd McConkey is being evaluated by the medical staff after suffering a head injury in the first half of the team’s Week 6 game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium. During the broadcast, it was announced that McConkey would be out for the remainder of the game. So far this season, McConkey has 12 catches for 183 yards and a touchdown as he has been dealing with a foot injury that put him on the injury report during the week. He was limited in the first two practices of the week but was a full participant on Friday and active for the game. Unfortunately, it appears the injury bug has stung him once again. McConkey’s foot injury caused him to leave the game early in Week 4 against the Seattle Seahawks, and he did not play in the team’s loss last week against the Denver Broncos. With McConkey getting evaluated for a concussion and Tre’ Harris out due to a hamstring injury, the team will rely on Quentin Johnston and KeAndre Lambert-Smith as its top receivers. Other players will need to step up across the offense in order for the team to try and win their first game of the season against the undefeated Chiefs. Otherwise, the Chargers could move to 0-6 on the season. The Chargers trail 9-3 against the Chiefs in the middle of the second quarter. Fans can watch the game on CBS or stream it on the Paramount Plus app.
